title: Between Decision and Dialogue: Ethical Limits and Practical Judgment in Labor Arbitration
affiliations: Ohio Northern University - Pettit College of Law

detail.title: Between Decision and Dialogue: Ethical Limits and Practical Judgment in Labor Arbitration

publicationDetails.detailsText: Labor Law Journal, Vol. 77, No. 2, pp. 75 et seq., summer 2026

detail.abstract: This essay examines when, if ever, a U.S. labor arbitrator may ethically encourage parties to pursue a negotiated resolution rather than proceed directly to an arbitral award. Drawing on comparative perspectives from Chinese commercial arbitration, Canadian labor arbitration, and U.S. public-sector factfinding, it questions the conventional American assumption that settlement facilitation is inherently inconsistent with the arbitrator’s decisional role. The essay identifies the principal ethical concerns raised by arbitral involvement in settlement—including coercion, confidentiality, role confusion, competence, and preservation of party autonomy—and argues that these concerns counsel restraint rather than categorical non-intervention. It then identifies recurring situations in which negotiation may better serve the parties than adjudication, including cases in which a nominal victory could produce harmful downstream consequences, contractual language restricts the arbitrator to unsatisfactory remedies, or an award would create unwanted precedent. Finally, the essay offers practical guidance for raising the possibility of negotiation without becoming a mediator, emphasizing transparency, neutrality, non-coercion, and respect for the parties’ continuing authority to resolve their own dispute.

title: Carbon Price Shocks and Emerging Market Equities: A Null Result on Cross-Border Spillovers from the EU ETS
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Carbon Price Shocks and Emerging Market Equities: A Null Result on Cross-Border Spillovers from the EU ETS
detail.abstract: This study empirically examines the impact of daily price shocks in the EUA futures market, which is the primary carbon pricing tool under the EU ETS, on stock market performance in four emerging countries that depend heavily on oil and natural resources, namely Brazil, India, Mexico, and South Africa. Using daily panel data from January 2022 through July 2026 (N = 3,924 countryday observations) and a fixed effects regression with date-clustered standard errors, the interaction between lagged EUA returns and oil rents in each country was not found to have a statistically significant effect on next-day equity returns (p = 0.945). Global stock market returns continue to dominate (β = 0.28, p < 0.001), and shocks to carbon prices do not appear to influence equity markets at daily frequencies.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Democracy: Elections, Disinformation and Constitutional Resilience

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Democracy: Elections, Disinformation and Constitutional Resilience
detail.abstract: Between 2023 and 2026, at least four legal systems adopted materially different responses to the same underlying problem: synthetic media capable of misrepresenting candidates, officials, and electoral processes. Brazil's Superior Electoral Court built a sector-specific, injunction-backed labeling and takedown regime; the European Union folded electoral synthetic media into a platform-level systemic-risk framework; South Korea enacted a blanket criminal prohibition operative in the ninety days preceding any election; and a California statute imposing civil liability for "materially deceptive" election content was preliminarily and then permanently enjoined as a content-based restriction failing strict scrutiny. This article asks why formally similar objectives produced such divergent doctrinal survival rates, and argues that the decisive variable is not the severity of the sanction but the object of regulation: interventions addressed to the provenance and distributional infrastructure of synthetic content have proven comparatively resilient to constitutional challenge, while interventions addressed to the truth-value of the content itself have not. Using doctrinal and comparative methods across Brazil, the European Union, the United States, and South Korea, the article traces this pattern through electoral-law resolutions, platform-regulation statutes, and constitutional adjudication, and develops the Electoral Information Provenance Standard (EIPS) as an analytical device for evaluating future AI-election measures. The article does not claim that provenance-based regulation is costless or immune from challenge; it argues, more modestly, that the choice of regulatory object-content or infrastructure-predicts constitutional durability more reliably than the choice of sanction, and that this has been underspecified in the existing literature on AI and democratic governance.

title: When Workforce Strategies Meet Credit Markets: The Impact of D&I on Credit Ratings
affiliations: Western Carolina University, California State University, San Bernardino and James Madison University - College of Business

detail.title: When Workforce Strategies Meet Credit Markets: The Impact of D&I on Credit Ratings
detail.abstract: This study examines whether and how workforce-related practices-specifically diversity and inclusion (D&I) initiatives-are incorporated into firms' credit risk assessments. Using a large panel of U.S. publicly listed firms, we find a robust and positive relationship between D&I performance and credit ratings, with the strongest effects observed when these practices function as a complementary and integrated system. Further analyses of the underlying mechanism show that the effect of D&I is stronger in firms characterized by greater information opacity and higher analyst coverage, but weaker in firms with higher agency costs, indicating that its value depends importantly on the firm's information environment and governance quality. These findings suggest that D&I serves as an informal governance mechanism by improving information flows, enhancing monitoring, and fostering organizational resilience. Overall, the evidence suggests that credit markets view D&I not as a symbolic initiative, but as a credible and economically meaningful signal of firm creditworthiness.

title: Beyond the $1 Billion Threshold: What Separates Credit Unions That Scale from Those That Stall?
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Beyond the $1 Billion Threshold: What Separates Credit Unions That Scale from Those That Stall?
detail.abstract: Crossing $1 billion in assets represents an important milestone for a credit union, but size alone is neither evidence of institutional maturity nor a guarantee of continued success. As credit unions move beyond this threshold, the organizational capabilities that enabled earlier expansion can become insufficient for managing greater complexity, regulatory expectations, technological demands, concentration risk, talent requirements, and changing member expectations. This article examines the transition beyond $1 billion as an institutional inflection point rather than simply a financial milestone. Drawing on contemporary credit union industry data, regulatory evidence, research on credit union growth and mergers, and recent organizational scholarship, it argues that sustainable scaling depends on the alignment of executive leadership, governance, organizational culture, enterprise risk management, technology, talent, integration capability, and member value creation. Growth creates a paradox for cooperative financial institutions: scale expands organizational capability while simultaneously increasing the potential for bureaucracy, cultural dilution, strategic distance from members, and slower decision-making. A conceptual model of scalable credit union leadership is introduced to explain why some institutions convert growth into sustainable organizational capacity while others encounter strategic and operational constraints. Ultimately, the article asks how a credit union can capture the economic advantages of scale without sacrificing the cooperative identity that provides its distinctive competitive advantage.

detail.abstract: Third-party cookies have historically enabled digital marketers to track user behavior across websites and optimize targeted advertising. However, increasing global privacy regulations and browser policy changes are accelerating the transition toward privacy-first marketing practices. Major web browsers are restricting or eliminating third-party cookies, requiring organizations to adopt alternative approaches to audience engagement. This paper examines the ongoing shift toward customer-centric digital marketing strategies, including first-party data collection, contextual advertising, and privacy-compliant analytics. The study synthesizes current literature to identify how marketers are adapting to a cookieless digital environment while maintaining effective audience targeting and compliance with data privacy regulations.

title: A Strategic Framework for U.S. Market Entry Among Global Personal Protective Equipment Sourcing Intermediaries Evidence from a Case Study of an International Industrial Safety Supplier

detail.title: A Strategic Framework for U.S. Market Entry Among Global Personal Protective Equipment Sourcing Intermediaries Evidence from a Case Study of an International Industrial Safety Supplier

declarations.ethicsApproval: Written consent for the case study was obtained from Varun Sharma of Promo Plus Textiles.

detail.abstract:
International sourcing intermediaries play an increasingly important role in global supply chains, yet limited research has examined how these firms can successfully enter highly regulated industrial markets. This paper develops a strategic framework for market entry into the United States among global personal protective equipment (PPE) sourcing intermediaries using an in-depth case study of Promo Plus Textiles, a Dubai-based intermediary seeking an expansion into the United States market. Examining strategic management principles, industry analysis, and market-entry theory, the study identifies the organization, regulatory, and competitive challenges faced by intermediary firms that coordinate international manufacturing rather than producing goods directly.

The analysis shows that competitive advantage for sourcing intermediaries is derived less from manufacturing capabilities than from supply chain coordination, regulatory compliance, supplier quality assurance, and relationship-based business development. Based on the case findings, this paper proposes a phased market-entry framework which puts an emphasis on regulatory alignment, targeted industry segmentation, strategic positioning, and progressive expansion from distributor partnerships toward direct enterprise sales. The framework illustrates how intermediary firms can transform global sourcing networks into sustainable competitive advantages while reducing perceived supply-chain risk among U.S. customers.

Although developed through a single case study, the framework that has been proposed offers a broader look at managerial implications for international sourcing firms pursuing entry into regulated business-to-business markets. The evidence contributes a practical decision-making model for executives and entrepreneurs while extending discussion of intermediary-based competitive strategy within global supply chain management.

title: How Money Could Move Us: Digital Payments and Interoperability Among Global Mass Transit Systems

detail.title: How Money Could Move Us: Digital Payments and Interoperability Among Global Mass Transit Systems

detail.abstract: Payments made towards mass transit systems are often such ubiquitous rituals in the lives of their users that their profound financial (and thereby social) influence goes overlooked. Across the globe, the decisions that mass transit providers make regarding which forms of currency to accept and validate are not only pivotal in enforcing physical boundaries by firmly dictating who needs what in order to go where when – but are ultimately key in establishing a precedent regarding which forms of currency are considered legitimate and, by extension, which authorities are recognized. This paper applies a qualitative comparative case study methodology across the fare payment systems in five major urban centers (New York, Hong Kong, Mexico City, Jakarta, and Nairobi) in order to document key themes in the adoption of digital fare payment. By examining the successes and failures of mass transit payment structures across distinct global contexts, this paper presents a comprehensive summary of how interoperable payment technologies enable greater economic and physical mobility – particularly for individuals outside of conventional banking structures. It demonstrates how various mass transit systems have moved to mirror evolving norms regarding payment and banking, and how this alignment with the average rider has in some cases enabled access and in others affirmed gaps.

title: A Misesian Theory of Statesmanship

detail.title: A Misesian Theory of Statesmanship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Ludwig von Mises is widely recognized for his contributions to economics, including a distinctive theory of entrepreneurship grounded in judgment under uncertainty. Far less recognized are Mises's views on political leadership and statesmanship. Because these views were never given systematic treatment, no recognized "Misesian" theory of statesmanship exists. I argue that such a theory can be reconstructed and contains original and underappreciated insights. Building on Mises's entrepreneurship framework, I show that his observations about political leadership cohere into a distinctive account in which the statesman acts under genuine uncertainty, exercises judgment about the long-run institutional consequences of ideas, and works to shape public opinion within the constraints it imposes. Critical disanalogies with market entrepreneurship, such as the absence of monetary calculation, the externalization of costs, and long feedback horizons, are distinctive features of Misesian statesmanship, yielding both positive predictions about how political leadership functions and normative implications about the statesman's primary duty to guide public opinion rather than manage policy. Misesian statesmanship offers a methodologically individualist account of how political agency sustains free societies, promoting material prosperity and human flourishing.

title: Re-Evaluating The Mandatory Three-Year Bar Practice Rule for Lower Judicial Service in India: A Socio-Legal and Policy Analysis

detail.title: Re-Evaluating The Mandatory Three-Year Bar Practice Rule for Lower Judicial Service in India: A Socio-Legal and Policy Analysis
detail.abstract:
In May 2025, a three-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India in All India Judges Association v. Union of India[1] restored the mandatory requirement of three years of active practice at the Bar (or judicial clerkship) as an essential prerequisite for appearing in the Civil Judge (Junior Division) competitive examinations. This decision overturned the long-standing 2002 precedent (AIJA II)[2] that had permitted fresh law graduates to directly enter the subordinate judiciary.

This research paper presents a comprehensive socio-legal and policy analysis of the three-year practice rule, evaluating its constitutional validity, institutional efficiency, and socio-economic ramifications. On one hand, institutional proponents argue that prior trial court practice develops crucial procedural instincts, judicial demeanor, and trial management skills under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)[3] and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)[4] that academic education alone cannot impart. On the other hand, the paper demonstrates how the rule acts as a severe structural barrier within India’s unorganized and largely uncompensated junior legal profession.

Using an intersectional analytical framework, this study highlights the disproportionate burden the mandate places on female candidates—threatening to reverse two decades of progress in gender representation by conflicting with societal and biological timelines—as well as first-generation lawyers, economically weaker sections, and aspirants from marginalized backgrounds who lack the financial "waiting power" to sustain unremunerated practice.

Finally, drawing on comparative international models, such as the German Referendariat system and the Indian Administrative Service (LBSNAA) institutional training framework, the paper proposes alternative policy solutions. It argues for a balanced approach that pairs open-entry examinations with stipend-supported pre-service judicial apprenticeships and paid clerkship equivalencies, thereby safeguarding judicial competence without compromising demographic diversity and substantive equality under Articles 14 and 16[5] of the Constitution of India.

title: Entropy Pooling with Relativistic Value at Risk Views
affiliations: Universidad Nacional de Ingeniería

detail.title: Entropy Pooling with Relativistic Value at Risk Views
detail.abstract: This work presents an extension of the entropy pooling approach to handle extreme views on the tails of the distribution of random variables. First, we provide the relativistic value at risk formulation for non uniform probabilities based on linear and power cone constraints. Second, we provide a formulation that allows the incorporation of absolute views on the relativistic value at risk into the traditional formulation of entropy pooling. Then, we run some numerical examples that show how these formulations allow to transform a prior distribution into a posterior distribution that incorporates relativistic value at risk views.

title:
The D-E-P Triangle

A Structural Theory of Direction, Execution, and Provision

detail.title:
The D-E-P Triangle

A Structural Theory of Direction, Execution, and Provision
detail.abstract: This paper develops the D-E-P triangle as a structural model of organizational power that begins before delegation. Within a problem-and-answer domain Q, D independently defines direction; E performs action created by authorization; and P receives the resulting product, service, or policy and decides whether to continue supplying the system. The model therefore separates autonomous offer formation, authorized execution, and voluntary selection. Principal-agent theory can analyze a constituted D-E edge, including repeated, multitask, and multiprincipal variants, but the dyad alone does not derive the initial formation of Q or the long-run renewal of the complete loop by P. The paper supplies ex ante role tests, distinguishes partial and collective D, and formalizes the D-E Dilemma: E selection rewards upward obedience, whereas D requires autonomous responsibility for Q before P. It then characterizes a reversible state space from the P-facing D-E-P limit, through the usual mixed D-E-DP structure, to E-P, in which organized E initiates and evaluates activity while managing P and restricting effective choice. Two further mechanisms complete the account. Unauthorized E innovation becomes programmatic only through D's ratification, and D's private service demands can be removed from the main loop through private-interest externalization and power separation. The framework is positive rather than moral: it identifies direction, execution, provision, evaluation, and responsibility without assigning substantive goodness to any actor or outcome.

detail.abstract:
Federal workforce programs place people successfully and cannot get them to finish. The Department of Labor reports that 91 percent of Registered Apprenticeship graduates retain employment, while its own 2021 equity report places completion below 35 percent for every racial group it reports. Job Corps graduates 32 percent of participants. A blended placement rate conceals this gap, and a cost model built on one hides the parameter that determines whether learners reach employment at all.

This paper responds with three contributions. First, it specifies a sequential competency architecture for K-12 STEM-EMCI content, organized around prerequisite ordering and verified mastery before advancement, and evidenced by federal assessment data showing thirteen year-old reading at approximately 1971 levels and mathematics at 1990 levels. Second, it proposes anchor-artifact pedagogy as a curriculum design method, in which one public-4 domain invention with active contemporary research literature carries multiple disciplinary strands. Three worked examples meet six stated selection criteria. Third, it supplies a bounded parameter framework in which every input carries a proposed value, a published range, a named federal source, and a stated conservatism position, with completion and post completion employment separated as distinct parameters.

The paper proposes no aggregate return figure, no program size, and no authorization period, because those quantities cannot be reproduced from their disclosed inputs. It restates five falsifiability thresholds set in advance by the author. One has been met: Bureau of Labor Statistics projections for 2024 to 2034 place STEM occupational growth below the stated threshold, and the affected employment projection is withdrawn. The comparative finding survives, with STEM occupations projected to grow at roughly 2.6 times the rate of all occupations. 

The architecture is voluntary and state-adoptable. Federal curriculum direction is prohibited by statute, and nothing proposed here creates a federal mandate.

title: Guidelines for End-User Prompt Writing for Data Retrieval Using Databricks Genie

detail.title: Guidelines for End-User Prompt Writing for Data Retrieval Using Databricks Genie
detail.abstract: Natural Language Interfaces for Databases (NLIDBs) have undergone a rapid evolution with the emergence of large language models (LLMs), significantly lowering the barrier for non-technical users to access and analyze structured enterprise data. Systems such as Databricks Genie exemplify this shift by enabling conversational data retrieval through natural language, yet empirical evidence consistently shows that query accuracy and reliability remain highly sensitive to prompt quality. This paper presents a comprehensive, user-centric set of guidelines for effective end-user prompt writing when interacting with Databricks Genie and similar LLM-powered text-to-SQL systems. Drawing on recent research in natural language processing, retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, and human-computer interaction, the guidelines synthesize best practices that improve query correctness, reduce ambiguity, and enhance system usability. The paper systematically addresses core principlesincluding clarity, context provision, schema awareness, and intent disambiguationalongside advanced techniques such as few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, structured prompt templates, and iterative refinement strategies. Special attention is given to complex analytical scenarios involving multi-table joins, aggregations, temporal reasoning, and domain-specific business logic, as well as privacy, governance, and performance considerations in enterprise environments. By translating technical research findings into practical, actionable guidance, this work demonstrates that end-user education in prompt formulation is a high-impact lever for improving self-service analytics, reducing reliance on technical specialists, and increasing trust in conversational data systems. The proposed guidelines provide a reusable framework for organizations seeking to operationalize natural language data access at scale.

detail.abstract: International development projects often suffer from a fundamental upstream problem: resources are allocated without sufficiently understanding the underlying constraints of the societies they aim to support. Existing project design processes rely heavily on top-down institutional perspectives, while conventional monitoring and evaluation focuses primarily on implementation and financial compliance rather than the causal validity of initial project choices. This paper proposes a Narrative-Based AI Bottleneck Finder, a framework that uses large-scale 1:1 stakeholder interviews and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to identify hidden causal relationships and structural bottlenecks before resources are allocated. The framework extracts causal statements from diverse stakeholder narratives, converts them into a directional Causal Knowledge Graph, and traces interconnected pathways to identify potential root constraints. A hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) layer further grounds these qualitative findings in independent macro-level data and analytical reports. By systematically incorporating grassroots narratives into development diagnostics, the proposed framework aims to reduce elite data capture, identify overlooked structural constraints, and improve the prioritization of limited development resources. The paper presents this architecture as a decision-support and upstream auditing mechanism, while recognizing that its causal validity and practical effectiveness require empirical testing. title: When Evidence-Based Governance Becomes Disconnected: From Production to Incorporation in U.S. State Governments

detail.title: When Evidence-Based Governance Becomes Disconnected: From Production to Incorporation in U.S. State Governments
detail.abstract: Do governments that successfully produce policy-relevant evidence also use it? This article examines that question through the National Youth in Transition Database (NYTD), a federally mandated longitudinal survey implemented by all 50 U.S. states. State performance in producing follow-up evidence varies sharply, with adjusted completion performance ranging from 29.0 to 87.4 percent. Crossing production performance with the depth of subsequent incorporation yields a four-part typology that distinguishes integrated evidence systems, production-oriented systems, use under production constraints, and thin evidence systems. The contrasts are substantial. Washington combines high production performance with deep downstream incorporation, while Arkansas combines weaker production with no documented substantive incorporation. More revealingly, Texas records the highest adjusted production performance in the country, yet its documented use remains concentrated in planning and organizational activity; Colorado, by contrast, shows substantially lower production performance but much deeper incorporation into policy and resource decisions. Drawing on three NYTD cohorts initiated in FY2011, FY2014, and FY2017, with follow-up observations extending through FY2021, and systematic analysis of public documentation of subsequent state use, the article shows that the institutional capacity to produce evidence and the organizational capacity to act on it are distinct. Institutionalizing evidence production does not automatically institutionalize evidence use.

detail.title: Musculoskeletal Disorder Risk Screening in Garment Sewing-Machine Operators: A Machine Learning Framework Using Dynamic Postural Exposure
detail.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) pose a significant occupational health challenge in labor-intensive industries, yet practical risk screening tools are limited. Sewing-machine operators face ergonomic risks from prolonged constrained sitting, repetitive arm movements, and forward neck flexion, which single-snapshot assessments may not fully capture. This study developed and internally evaluated a machine learning based framework to classify garment sewing-machine operators in Bangladesh into low-, medium-, and high-WMSD risk groups. Sixty sewing operators completed video recordings of bilateral tasks and a modified Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (mNMQ). Frame-wise joint angles were extracted and converted into time-weighted RULA scores to represent cumulative postural exposure. The SEP-based MSD Index was used to define the target risk class, while dynamic time-weighted RULA scores and selected demographic, physiological, and work-organization variables were used as predictor features. Eight machine learning classifiers were evaluated using stratified cross-validation, with SMOTE applied within each training fold. WMSD prevalence was 96.7%, with neck pain the most commonly reported complaint (91.7%). Time-weighted RULA scores were strongly correlated with the MSD Index (r = 0.77, p < 0.001). Random Forest achieved the highest internal classification accuracy (98.33%) and showed strong sensitivity across all three risk strata, including the high-risk group. Gender-stratified analysis showed broadly comparable classification accuracy across male and female subgroups, though small subgroup sizes limit firm conclusions. The internally evaluated framework provides a practical approach for factory-floor WMSD risk screening, supporting early identification of high-risk workers and guiding targeted ergonomic interventions, subject to external validation in larger and more diverse samples.

title: Grand Strategy in Interregnum: Systemic Crises and the Transformation of Great-Power Order, 2020–2026

detail.abstract: Between 2020 and 2026 the international system absorbed a sequence of shocks-a global pandemic, a chaotic Western withdrawal from Afghanistan, a full-scale interstate war in Europe, two rounds of direct US-Israeli-Iranian warfare, and a hardening Sino-Russian entente-that together raise a basic question for the study of grand strategy: has this crisis cascade produced a genuine transformation of great-power order, or has it merely accelerated trends already underway before 2020? This article develops an explicit, ex-ante coding protocol for distinguishing reinforcement, adaptation, redefinition, and rupture in grand strategy, operationalized across material and ideational indicators with named thresholds, and applies it through structured comparison of the United States, China, and Russia, with the European Union examined as a deliberately harder, partially disconfirming case. It argues that the period is best characterized neither as orderly transition to multipolarity nor as resilient continuation of the post-Cold War order, but as a genuine interregnum: the old order's institutional shell persists while its animating consensus has eroded faster than any successor arrangement has consolidated. The United States codes as redefinition; China as reinforcement-with-intensification; Russia as redefinition imposed by material failure; the European Union, more ambiguously, as largely reinforcement, complicating any reading of the interregnum thesis as self-confirming. The article specifies observable conditions that would disconfirm the thesis, distinguishes systemic interregnum pressure from administration-contingent policy swing in the American case, and incorporates a constructivist account of norm erosion to strengthen the framework's ideational half. It concludes that the interregnum is characterized by contested and unevenly institutionalized multipolarity, elevated risk of miscalculation, and a widening gap between the pace of material change and the pace of normative adjustment.

title: Women's Education, Marriage and Fertility Behavior in Uganda: Evidence from Universal Secondary Education Policy

detail.title: Women's Education, Marriage and Fertility Behavior in Uganda: Evidence from Universal Secondary Education Policy
detail.abstract: This study sheds light on the Universal Secondary Education (USE) policy in Uganda and examines its impacts on educational attainment and fertility behaviors, including first sexual intercourse, marriage and childbirth, among adolescent women in Uganda. The analysis employs a continuous difference-in-differences framework to estimate the local average treatment effect of the policy, using pre-policy educational and economic conditions as proxies for policy intensity. The findings are twofold. First, the USE policy significantly increased women’s educational attainment: the extent of the increase was greater for those in disadvantaged areas who could be considered the main beneficiaries of the policy. Second, however, while adolescent sexual activities, marriages, and childbirths declined over time surrounding the policy implementation, the decline is not attributable to the USE policy: these behaviors declined less in disadvantaged areas where the policy increased educational attainment. This study further explores the possibility of a nonlinear relationship between education and fertility behaviors: that is, increases in education may affect fertility behaviors only when educational attainment reaches a sufficiently high level. This highlights the importance of education policies increasing educational attainment to a sufficient level.

title: Wartime Origins of Social Policy: How Contraband Camps Shaped Redistributive Programs in the U.S. South
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor and Virginia Tech - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Wartime Origins of Social Policy: How Contraband Camps Shaped Redistributive Programs in the U.S. South
detail.abstract: One of the most important developments of the modern nation-state is its expansion to provide redistributive and social welfare programs. Yet, these programs vary considerably both nationally and subnationally. Why? Focusing on the U.S. South after the Civil War, a region with notoriously limited redistributive social programs, we argue that the wartime policy of contraband camps explains important variation in social welfare policies. Contraband camps involved investments in physical institutions, civilian leadership in camp administration, and high levels of exposure to redistributive and abolitionist ideas within camp communities. These three processes were highly concentrated in contraband camp counties and made postwar investments in redistributive social policy more likely. We test our arguments using new data, including full-count censuses. Results strongly support expectations: counties with a contraband camp had about a 74% increase in tax revenue compared to counties without one. Our results contribute to research on U.S. political development, redistributive social policies, war, and post-con!ict reconstruction.

title: Dichotomization in Bayesian Binary Classification
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: Dichotomization in Bayesian Binary Classification
detail.abstract: Classification problems are routinely simplified by dichotomizing a continuum of states into two categories, e.g., creditworthy/not, guilty/innocent, high-type/low-type. This dichotomization is not a form of Blackwell garbling, because it leaves the experiment itself untouched. Whether it leads to losses is an open question, which this paper answers. When the laws of evidence are known and affine in payoffs, every dichotomization is lossless. Otherwise, dichotomization generates losses only when the utility-prominence comovements are unbalanced across the two dichotomized categories. Ex-ante indifference then ensures that some lossless dichotomization exists, and simple symmetry conditions guarantee that dichotomization through the natural beneficial-harmful state split is lossless. Outside the lossless region, I measure losses as a share of the cost of uncertainty in the normal-prior-normal-signal environment. Losses vanish as base rates become balanced, and they are largest with extreme base rates and intermediately informative signals.

title: Deep learning-based automatic global alignment of intraoral 3D dental models
affiliations: Yeditepe University and Yeditepe University

detail.title: Deep learning-based automatic global alignment of intraoral 3D dental models
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Alignment of 3D dental models is a critical component of digital workflows where initial alignment is often manual. Existing methods such as Iterative Closest Point or Principal Component Analysis fails under large initial misalignments due to local minima entrapment and sign ambiguity, respectively. This study proposes a deep learning-based framework for fully automatic global alignment of 3D dental models. Methods: A single 3D dental model, which is the target for registration, is used to train the system. The training data were generated by applying random rigid transformations to the point cloud of this target dental model, covering the full rotation range of 0o-180o and translations up to 10 mm. A PointNet-based neural network was developed to regress 6-DoF rigid transformation parameters directly from unaligned point clouds in a single forward pass.A continuous 6D rotation representation combined with a Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization layer ensures mathematically valid outputs on the SO(3) manifold. Results: On unseen test subjects, the proposed method achieves mean rotation errors of 5.73o and 9.34o for the maxilla and mandible, respectively, compared to over 84o for both ICP and PCA. The method reaches approximately 90% success within a 10o rotation threshold for the maxilla, with an inference time under 5 ms. In the local alignment range (0o-30o), ICP achieves lower rotation errors but requires significantly longer inference times. Conclusions: The proposed learning-based framework reliably solves the global alignment problem where classical methods systematically fail due to geometric symmetry and initialization sensitivity. The low inference time makes it suitable for integration into real-time digital dentistry workflows.

detail.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces but does not eliminate unsupported assertions in language-model systems, because in the common implementation the model authors both the answer and its source reference. This paper draws a distinction between a model-authored citation (a generated claim about provenance) and a record-carried citation (a data field attached to a retrieved record independently of any generated text). We define a citation soundness property over displayed outputs, show that it is enforceable by a deterministic validation gate operating after inference and before display, and argue that the gate must fail closed rather than degrade. The formal content is definitional rather than deep; the contribution is architectural, and its value is that it converts a per-instance verification question into an operation a third party can perform without access to the system. We describe an implementation in a production consumer decision system, report the citation-resolvability profile of its curated corpus, and set out the two prerequisites on which the guarantee depends.

title: U.S. Secondary Sanctions on Iran and China’s Countermeasures: From Meng Wanzhou to Hengli

detail.title: U.S. Secondary Sanctions on Iran and China’s Countermeasures: From Meng Wanzhou to Hengli
detail.abstract: U.S. sanctions on Iran have a China problem: if China keeps buying Iranian oil, “maximum pressure” can’t work without targeting the Chinese refiners, shippers, traders, and banks that keep the trade moving. In 2026, Washington designated Hengli—one of China’s biggest independent refineries—and Beijing hit back in a first-of-its-kind move by activating its 2021 Blocking Rules, ordering that the U.S. measures not be “recognized, enforced, or complied with.” This paper traces how the 2018 Meng Wanzhou case jolted China into building a full counter-sanctions toolkit—both “sword” and “shield”—and argues that Hengli marks the moment it became operational. The result: a new era of sanctions warfare where U.S. pressure on Iran increasingly triggers direct U.S.–China conflicts of law—and global firms get caught in the crossfire.

title:

A Practical Guide for Financial Institutions

detail.title:
The Compatibility of Permissionless Networks and Financial Integrity
A Practical Guide for Financial Institutions
detail.abstract: Regulated financial institutions are building new products on blockchain-based infrastructure at a rapid pace, recognizing the pro-competitive benefits offered by this new technology. Some of these institutions, however, have opted for permissioned versions of this infrastructure, and treat open, permissionless blockchain networks-one of the most novel innovations in this category-as unavailable to them due to concerns about financial integrity. Some institutions voice that transacting on a network maintained by pseudonymous, globally distributed validators with other pseudonymous participants cannot be reconciled with their obligations relating to anti-money laundering ("AML"), countering the financing of terrorism ("CFT") and U.S. sanctions. This paper argues that those concerns are not well-founded, and that financial institutions can build and use permissionless networks in compliance with their obligations under the Bank Secrecy Act ("BSA") and its attendant amendments as well as the sanctions laws. To that end, institutions can update their compliance programs with robust financial integrity risk management controls, like those set forth in this paper, for use of permissionless systems. Specifically, the paper (1) explains the differences between permissionless and permissioned networks; (2) demonstrates the compatibility of permissionless networks with the BSA and U.S. sanctions laws, noting that nothing in current law requires a permissioned validator set or group of participants; (3) answers the objections most commonly raised by regulated institutions, including exposure to illicit actors at the network layer, the confidentiality of onchain data, the provenance of assets whose transaction history touches an illicit actor, and the compatibility of data privacy and compliance; and (4) sets forth a risk-management framework under which institutions place compliance controls at the application layer (which they operate and control), rather than at the network layer. Finally, this paper discusses the benefits that accrue from permissionless networks: the same benefits that will accrue to institutions and others alike, on the same terms, given the credibly neutral architecture of permissionless networks.

The traditional model, built around geographical fragmentation, functional specialization, and cost-efficiency outsourcing, is increasingly challenged by a new regulatory and technological environment shaped by resilience, accountability, and control. The evolution of supply chains in the European Union is driven by the intersection of two closely connected developments: the growing centrality of digital technologies and data value chains, and the emergence of mandatory sustainability due diligence obligations. title: Economic Shocks and Income Polarization under Quasi-Marketization: Evidence from North Korea
affiliations: Bank of Korea

detail.title: Economic Shocks and Income Polarization under Quasi-Marketization: Evidence from North Korea

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Korea Economic Research Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how adverse economic shocks reshape the income distribution in an economy characterized by quasi-marketization, where market activities expand in the absence of fully institutionalized market-supporting institutions. Using repeated cross-sectional survey data on North Korean defectors from 2012 to 2020, the analysis exploits a plausibly exogenous economic shock during 2014–2015 in North Korea driven by climatic conditions, energy supply constraints, and external trade disruptions. Focusing on changes in distributional shape rather than average inequality, the paper employs the Median Relative Polarization framework and relative distribution analysis. The results show a significant increase in informal income polarization in the post-shock period, driven primarily by an expansion of the lower tail of the distribution rather than by gains at the top. A range of robustness checks indicates that these findings are not solely driven by sample selection. The findings highlight that in quasi-marketized economies without established market-supporting institutions (i.e., fair competition policies, taxation, and social safety nets), adverse shocks may generate asymmetric distributional adjustments—manifesting primarily as lower-tail polarization—rather than uniform increases in inequality.

title: Closing the Gap: A Provincial Framework for Menopause Health in Ontario

detail.title: Closing the Gap: A Provincial Framework for Menopause Health in Ontario

detail.abstract: British Columbia and Manitoba have both moved to cover menopause hormone therapy through their public drug plans. Ontario has not. Transdermal estrogen and micronized progesterone are frequently recommended for women with an elevated risk of venous thromboembolism, since current evidence indicates a lower VTE risk with the transdermal route than with oral estrogen in appropriate patients. Oral estrogen remains a reasonable choice for many other women. Ontario women who already qualify for the Ontario Drug Benefit program may seek case-by-case coverage of the transdermal route through the Exceptional Access Program; women who are not ODB-eligible have no such option and pay for it themselves. This paper lays out a five-part framework, built by Menopause Matter, for closing that gap: drug coverage, physician training, better data, workplace support, and a clearer path to care. It identifies the administrative mechanism, already in place under the Ontario Drug Benefit Act, through which this change can be evaluated without new primary legislation, and provides a transparent, scenario-based estimate of the likely fiscal scale.

title: Limits of State Protection? Emigration States and Interstate Diplomacy During the Covid-19 Pandemic in the Gulf

detail.title: Limits of State Protection? Emigration States and Interstate Diplomacy During the Covid-19 Pandemic in the Gulf
detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on emigration states’ migration governance framework, with a specific focus on onsite diplomatic practices and strategies in protecting migrant workers’ rights and welfare in the UAE. Based on preliminary field interviews with senior officials, diaspora community leaders and migrant workers from the Philippines and Nepal, based in the UAE, we argue that the pandemic has not only further limited onsite diplomatic protection, but also largely widened the prevailing power asymmetry between states, thus collectively generating a spectrum of migrant vulnerabilities in the host country.

We divide this chapter into three sections. First, we examine the role of emigration states in the context of global migration diplomacy and crisis. Second, we explore two emigration states— the Philippines and Nepal—and investigate how the Covid-19 pandemic has had a structural impact on their foreign policy, specifically onsite diplomatic practices and strategies in the UAE, as well as on their domestic policy responses to the pandemic. Third, we analyze how emigration states’ structural limits have simultaneously (dis)empowered community diasporic groups and, in some cases, produced political conflict both in virtual and physical mobilization settings. The concluding section summarizes the potential effects of the pandemic on emigration states’ bargaining power, interests and status in the UAE and the GCC countries.

title: Climate Shocks and Property Rights to Land.
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Bologna and

detail.title: Climate Shocks and Property Rights to Land.

keywords: public good provision. JEL classification: D72

detail.abstract: While the direct economic effects of adverse climate shocks are well-known, their indirect institutional impact is still unclear. To shed light on this issue, we focus on the most agricultural countries, and we test the idea that adverse climate shocks push elites unable to commit to future transfers to grant the non-elites strong property rights to land to convince them that a sufficient part of the returns on common farming innovations would be shared via public good provision. Consistent with this prediction, data on a panel of 38-among the 42-most agricultural countries observed over the 1960-2018 period imply that the severity of droughts has both the negative and direct effect of reducing agricultural output and the positive and indirect impact of shielding the non-elites' land from the elites' expropriation. In turn, reforms towards stronger non-elites' property rights to land foster the diffusion of contracts strengthening the peasants' land tenure, encourage the adoption of wheel and crawler tractors and shift the allocation of the tax revenues from military to public health service expenditures. Crucially, these results hold across several identification strategies.

title: Access to Standards, Access to Markets: ISO Access, Quality Infrastructure, and International Trade
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology - Faculty of Economics and Business Management and

detail.title: Access to Standards, Access to Markets: ISO Access, Quality Infrastructure, and International Trade
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether access to the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) increases trade and through which margin. Using newly constructed ISO access data in a domestic-inclusive structural gravity framework for 185 trading partners from 1980 to 2016, the paper shows that ISO access increases international trade relative to domestic trade. Trade involving one ISO access country is about 63 percent higher than trade between countries without ISO access, while trade between two ISO access countries is about 95 percent higher. The effects are more visible for less developed countries and are stronger when the ISO access country is the exporter. Evidence on ISO certification uptake is consistent with an exporter-side standardization and certification-capacity channel. The paper identifies ISO access as an upstream quality infrastructure channel of trade. The findings imply that standardization and certification capacity can help countries overcome non-tariff barriers and upgrade exports.

title: Comparisons
affiliations: and Harvard University

detail.title: Comparisons
detail.abstract: Economic decisions are often shaped by comparison points such as reference points, goals, expectations and peers. A long-standing puzzle is that decisions sometimes increase in these comparators (assimilation) and sometimes decrease in them (contrast). We develop a simple taxonomy that predicts the sign. The idea is that when absolute evaluations - translating a decision input into an output - are difficult, people use comparison points as information about how to navigate tradeoffs. This logic predicts that decisions decrease in input comparators - those tied to exogenous decision inputs (e.g., a typical hourly wage) - and increase in output comparators - those tied to endogenous decisions or outcomes (e.g., typical daily earnings). We test and confirm these predictions in experiments on labor supply, investment and belief updating, involving both social and expectations-based comparison points. We further show that comparison effects weaken both when decision uncertainty is experimentally reduced and when comparators are less informative, consistent with a mechanism of comparisons as information. Finally, a classification of the prior literature suggests that the input-vs.-output taxonomy organizes the sign of comparison effects across more than 100 experimental and field observational studies.

title: AI Persuasion and Financial-Decision Making: Experimental Evidence on Dominated Investment Choices
affiliations: ,  and University of Bayreuth - Faculty of Law, Business and Economics

detail.title: AI Persuasion and Financial-Decision Making: Experimental Evidence on Dominated Investment Choices
detail.abstract: In an online experiment, we study how generative AI steers individuals toward dominated choices and, conversely, helps them avoid such mistakes. Participants choose between two virtual index funds, one of which strictly dominates the other. An AI chatbot increases optimal choices by over 20 percentage points when promoting the optimal fund but reduces them by almost 30 points when promoting the dominated fund. Its influence is undiminished when framed as bank-provided despite a disclosed interest. Incentivized human advice steers choices toward the promoted fund but is significantly less effective. Transcript analyses tentatively suggest that AI's advantage reflects more persuasive argumentation.

title: Geopolitics and Export Miracles: Firm-Level Evidence from U.S. War Procurement in Korea
affiliations: , ,  and University of Oxford, Saïd Business School

detail.title: Geopolitics and Export Miracles: Firm-Level Evidence from U.S. War Procurement in Korea
detail.abstract: How did geopolitics shape East Asia's economic development? We find that U.S. military procurement during the Vietnam War — a shock which peaked at nearly 3% of South Korean GDP, rivaling the Marshall Plan — catalyzed Korea's export-led industrialization. We construct a new firm-level dataset that matches Korean export records with U.S. procurement contracts awarded between 1965 and 1974 to estimate the causal impact of winning a contract on export performance. A firm winning its first contract raises its likelihood of exporting by 14.7 percentage points and its export value by 40%. Treated firms are more likely to expand into third-country markets and export manufacturing products — and these gains are unlikely to come from business stealing. Finally, we find that U.S. procurement and domestic industrial policy were likely complementary. Our findings reveal a neglected channel through which Cold War geopolitics shaped the East Asian economic miracle.

title: The Pass-Through of Sales Tax Exemptions: Evidence from Menstrual Hygiene Products

detail.title: The Pass-Through of Sales Tax Exemptions: Evidence from Menstrual Hygiene Products
detail.abstract: This paper examines how sales tax exemptions for menstrual hygiene products affect prices, using NielsenIQ Consumer Panel Data from 2004 to 2022. I estimate the pass-through of sales tax repeal using two complementary designs. First, I implement a staggered differencein-differences framework that exploits variation in policy timing across 18 states. Second, I estimate a triple-differences specification that additionally exploits variation across products by comparing period products with deodorants, whose tax treatment is unchanged. I find that the pass-through rate ranges from 94% to 100%, implying that sales tax exemptions are nearly fully or fully passed through to consumer prices. These findings indicate that removing sales taxes on menstrual products can increase affordability and help reduce period poverty.

title: Train Stations and Car Registrations: Evidence from Station Openings in Germany
affiliations: , ,  and Technology University of Braunschweig

detail.title: Train Stations and Car Registrations: Evidence from Station Openings in Germany
detail.abstract: Does better railway infrastructure encourage people to register less private cars? We analyse the opening of 170 train stations in Germany between 2010 and 2022 and compare them to a control group of locations that were identified as potential sites for new stations. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that annual car registrations within the catchment area of a newly opened station decline by at least 3.5 to 5.5 percent permanently. These effects are consistent in both urban and rural settings and correspond, on average, to at least 140 fewer car registrations over ten years for each new station. Further evidence suggests that the effects are driven by habit changes rather than by spatial sorting, leading to the conclusion that new train stations reduce the number of car registrations both locally and globally.

title: The Dark Swan of Capitalism: The Political Economy of the Pandemic and the Mechanism of Crisis Reproduction

detail.title: The Dark Swan of Capitalism: The Political Economy of the Pandemic and the Mechanism of Crisis Reproduction
detail.abstract: The article proposes a new analytical category-the "Dark Swan"-for the critical examination of global crises in the era of late capitalism. Taking as their point of departure the popular concept of the "black swan" (N. Taleb) as an external and unpredictable event, the authors argue that certain contemporary catastrophes, the COVID-19 pandemic being the case in point, are immanent to the system and perform within it the function of a catalyst and accelerant of its fundamental contradictions. A political-economic analysis of the pandemic brings to light three key conflicts (Capital vs. Labour, Large vs. Small Capital, the Biopolitical State vs. the Social State), demonstrating that the crisis was no force majeure but became an instrument for the accelerated redistribution of risks, the concentration of wealth, the growth of inequality, and the legitimation of unprecedented instruments of digital control and surveillance. At the theoretical level, the article substantiates the systemic necessity of "Dark Swans" for capitalism. They operate as a mechanism of its crisis reproduction (in the political-economic sense), serving as: (1) an "external" response to the immanent tendency of the rate of profit to fall; (2) an operational means of "accumulation by dispossession" (D. Harvey), transferring public goods into private hands; (3) a key political technology of the "shock doctrine" (N. Klein) for the implementation of unpopular neoliberal reforms; and (4) an internal operation of an autopoietic system (N. Luhmann) converting any chaos into fuel for accumulation. A historical retrospective (the collapse of the USSR, September 11, 2001, the financial crisis of 2008) confirms that the pandemic stands within a series of systemic events, each of which was used for a qualitative leap toward a greater concentration of power, capital, and control. The article contributes to critical political economy by outlining a methodology that shifts the focus from the management of crises to the analysis of their exploitation as an immanent function of the capitalist system.

While recent literature on diagnosis-contingent contracts demonstrates that conditioning treatment subsidies on verified diagnostic testing can curb overtreatment, these models typically adopt a single-sided perspective (e.g., patient price discounts or retail pharmacy margins). This paper formulates a dynamic, multi-stakeholder microeconomic equilibrium model that unifies all five primary healthcare actors: Patients, Insurers (Payers), Healthcare Providers and Staff, Pharmaceutical Manufacturers, and Government/Public Health entities. By integrating zero-copay digital triaging, continuous biomarker precision subsidies (s d (0 ˆ)), indication-specific drug pricing, and risk-adjusted capitation pools with shared savings (y), we prove that the structural waste eliminated from low-value procedures (25%-30% of total spending) can be redistributed to achieve a simultaneous Pareto improvement (ΔU k > 0 for all k).

title: Prior Sentiment and Returns Around Earnings Announcements
affiliations: and

detail.title: Prior Sentiment and Returns Around Earnings Announcements
detail.abstract: We develop a stylized model in which sentiment-driven demand creates a pre-announcement price wedge that is harder for arbitrageurs to offset when fundamental uncertainty is high. The model predicts that prior sentiment shifts expected post-announcement returns separately from the earnings surprise and that the shift is larger when firm-level and aggregate sentiment align. We test these predictions using LSEG MarketPsych sentiment, I/B/E/S earnings surprises, and CRSP returns for 83,293 U.S. quarterly earnings announcements from 1998-2022. The 10-day low-minus-high cumulative abnormal-return spread is 1.38 percentage points for firm-level sentiment and 1.50 percentage points for aggregate sentiment. Sentiment enters separately from the earnings surprise, while sentiment-by-surprise interactions are generally small and statistically insignificant. The return spread is larger when analyst forecasts are noisier and when firm-level and aggregate sentiment have the same sign. Firm-level sentiment predicts a smaller spread on randomly selected non-announcement dates, while aggregate sentiment has little explanatory power on those dates. The results isolate the predictive content of daily pre-announcement sentiment from the immediate response to realized earnings news and show how it varies with valuation uncertainty and sentiment source.

title: Dynamic Contracting under Regime-Switching Learning
affiliations: School of Business, Southern University of Science and Technology, China and Southern University of Science and Technology - Department of Finance

detail.title: Dynamic Contracting under Regime-Switching Learning
detail.abstract: We address a dynamic contracting problem in which investors hire a manager to operate a project whose profitability switches between high and low regimes that are not directly observable by both investors and the manager. Cash flows are also affected by the manager's hidden diversion, creating an attribution problem: investors may interpret poor performance caused by diversion as a deterioration in the project's underlying profitability. This misattribution generates an endogenous information rent for the manager. We show that the information rent is a deterministic function of the manager's promised value and the posterior belief about profitability. The resulting information-rent premium is the product of the information rent and the signal-to-noise ratios associated with regime switching and Bayesian learning, increasing with the profitability spread and with belief uncertainty and decreasing with the total switching intensity. Methodologically, reducing the investor's optimization from three states to two, we specify an optimal contract by the joint determination of the payment boundary and the information rent. We further show that the optimal contract can be implemented through a standard LBO capital structure.

detail.abstract:
Respirable crystalline silica (RCS), the quartz fraction of respirable mineral dust, is a leading cause of occupational lung disease and is regulated at an 8-hour time-weighted-average (TWA) exposure standard of 0.05 mg/m3 in Australia, with a scheduled tightening to a lower, legally enforceable limit from December 2026, mirroring recent tightening in South Africa (2025) and the United States (MSHA, 2024). The statutory measurement is laboratory gravimetric sampling with XRD or IR quantification: one worker per exposure group, a single 8-hour number returned days-to-weeks later at material cost. There is no accepted continuous direct-reading RCS monitor: direct silica measurement needs mass separation and elemental analysis, neither portable nor fast.

We frame continuous RCS monitoring as an inference problem: RCS is estimated as respirable-dust concentration x silica fraction x optical-to-gravimetric correction, and machine learning is used to infer the two variable terms from adjacent, continuously-sensed signals and to calibrate the estimate against accredited gravimetric-reference pairs. This is the design of the SilicaSense model. This paper does not present gravimetric-validation results; it characterises, on a five-week on-board sensing pilot at an anonymised surface mine in Western Australia (22,802 records; mass and number PM1/PM2.5/PM4/PM10, particle size, kinematics, environment, geolocation) that lacked paired gravimetric labels, the four properties the model relies on, all pre-specified.

(1) The respirable-dust channel is operationally valid. Mean respirable dust (PM4) fell 1097 to 220 ug/m3 (-80%) across a water-suppression intervention.

(2) The particle-size signature carries source information (F1). Concentration-invariant shape features resolve three interpretable dust states (respirable-mass means 19 / 72 / 664 ug/m3). Silica has a distinct, coarser size distribution than total dust, so this is the physical basis for a learned, source-aware silica fraction.

(3) Multi-source inference tightens the estimate (F2, headline). Under leakage-safe day-grouped cross-validation, respirable dust is inferable from fused operational context alone (10 sources, no dust channel) at R2 = 0.49, rising to R2 = 0.73 with the optical size signature, versus 0.45 for the best single indicator. The size signature (45%) and speed (26%) dominate; accelerometer/gyroscope contribute approximately 0% (a reported null).

(4) The silica fraction is the dominant uncertainty (F3), confirmed on accredited data. Propagating literature-grounded ranges, a single-factor RCS estimate for representative dust spans 2.9-84.2 ug/m3 (29x fold-range), straddling the 50 ug/m3 standard, with the silica fraction contributing approximately 79% of the variance. Grounding this on 146,112 accredited paired samples from the US MSHA databases, the silica fraction of respirable dust has a geometric SD of 2.41 (35x fold-range), a single fixed fraction mis-predicts per-sample RCS by a median 46%, and the empirically-grounded estimate uncertainty widens to a 43x fold-range with the fraction contributing 84% of the variance. This is precisely why the fraction must be inferred per material-domain and calibrated against gravimetric pairs, not assumed from a single site factor.

We are explicit about scope: this is a measurement-framework and feasibility study on an un-labelled pilot, not a silica-accuracy claim. We describe the gravimetric-pair calibration the deployed model uses and register the prospective validation that would quantify accuracy (pre-registration doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/87N9C), and release the frozen data and code under CC-BY 4.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22040688).

title: Data-Efficient Cross-Subject Emotion Recognition Using Hybrid ECG Representations and Active Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Data-Efficient Cross-Subject Emotion Recognition Using Hybrid ECG Representations and Active Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation
detail.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG)-based emotion recognition has emerged as a promising approach for affective computing; however, subject-independent recognition remains challenging because inter-subject variability in cardiac dynamics introduces a significant domain shift between training and unseen subjects. To address this problem, we propose a hybrid semi-supervised domain adaptation framework that integrates wavelet-based time-frequency features with deep representations learned from raw ECG signals, enabling complementary modeling of spectral and temporal cardiac characteristics. The framework combines domain-adversarial learning with pseudo-label refinement to learn emotion-discriminative and subject-invariant representations from labeled source and unlabeled target data. In addition, an active learning strategy is incorporated to efficiently identify informative target samples for annotation, improving adaptation under limited supervision. The proposed method is evaluated on the DREAMER dataset for subject-independent arousal and valence classification. Ablation studies demonstrate the complementary contributions of domain-adversarial learning, pseudo-label refinement, semi-supervised adaptation, and active learning, with performance consistently improving as additional labeled target samples become available. The proposed approach achieves its best performance with accuracies of 74.2% (macro-F1: 72.8%) for arousal and 73.9% (macro-F1: 71.1%) for valence, substantially outperforming the source-only baseline. These findings demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates domain shift and enables cross-subject ECG emotion recognition with minimal target-domain supervision.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scalable and Reliable Fog-Edge Resource Orchestration in Software-Defined Networks

detail.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scalable and Reliable Fog-Edge Resource Orchestration in Software-Defined Networks
detail.abstract: The proliferation of ultra-low-latency and computationally demanding services ranging from autonomous vehicular networks and industrial digital twins to tele-surgery and immersive extended reality-has rendered conventional cloudcentric models inadequate. Although the fusion of software-defined networking (SDN) with fog-edge computing offers a promising decentralized and programmable infrastructure, current resource management approaches suffer from three fundamental shortcomings: (i) centralised controllers that become bottlenecks under massive heterogeneity, (ii) heuristic-driven policies that cannot deliver strict quality-of-service (QoS) bounds, and (iii) fragility under node failures and bursty traffic fluctuations. To address these challenges, we propose HARMONIC a novel hierarchical multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework that achieves scalable, resilient, and QoS-aware orchestration in SDN-enabled fog-edge networks.
