title: The Plate Is Not the Person: What Owner Liability Already Concedes About Automated Vehicle Surveillance

detail.title: The Plate Is Not the Person: What Owner Liability Already Concedes About Automated Vehicle Surveillance
detail.abstract: A camera at the roadside records a registration plate. A database converts that record into an assertion about where a person has been. Nothing in the pipeline verifies that the person was ever in the vehicle. This article names that conversion silent attribution, names the space it crosses the attribution gap, and argues that American law has already adjudicated both, where no one has looked. Automated traffic enforcement concedes the premise three times. Illinois supplies defenses when a vehicle or its plates were stolen and therefore "not under the control of or in the possession of the owner," language a legislature writes only when it knows the owner is frequently not the driver. The Seventh Circuit upheld owner liability in Idris v. City of Chicago on the reasoning that a camera reliably shows which vehicles ran a light but is less likely to show who was driving, leaving a city essentially unable to prove otherwise. And in Tupper v. City of St. Louis the Supreme Court of Missouri struck down a camera ordinance for creating a presumption that shifted the burden of persuasion onto the owner to prove he was not the operator. Plate reader doctrine has developed as though none of that existed. Courts ask whether a plate is exposed to public view and whether accumulated location points reconstruct the whole of a person's movements. Both questions presuppose that the vehicle's movements are the person's, and the leading decisions do not defend that premise because they never reach it. Kansas v. Glover authorized the inference for reasonable suspicion alone, only absent contrary information, and only where an officer looking at the driver can dispel it. Database retrieval removes all three. The article then tests the justification the networks are sold on. Substituting a plate defeats a reader more cheaply than avoiding one, and it does not produce invisibility. It produces misdirection onto a registered owner who was never present, which the system cannot detect and which the falsely named owner learns by mail. The contributions are three. It locates a statutory and judicial admission that a plate does not identify a driver, sitting in the jurisdictions that treat plate data as location history. It shows that no stage of retrieval records the moment a vehicle observation becomes a claim about a person. And it identifies the class whose recorded travel is false in its entirety: registered owners who do not drive.

title: Differing Environmental Preferences, Fiscal Competition, and Taxation of Goods and Pollution
affiliations: Toulouse Business School, University of Toulouse (GREMAQ & IDEI) and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Economics

detail.title: Differing Environmental Preferences, Fiscal Competition, and Taxation of Goods and Pollution
detail.abstract: We develop a two-country model of trade and global pollution in which country A values environmental quality whereas country B does not. Governments choose emissions and commodity taxes non-cooperatively under autarky and free trade. Under autarky, the principle of targeting holds: country A levies a Pigouvian emissions tax, whereas neither country uses a commodity tax. Opening borders fundamentally changes the design of corrective taxation. Country A subsidizes the polluting good to shift production toward its cleaner firms. The optimal subsidy depends on the marginal social damage of emissions despite the presence of an emissions tax, implying a violation of the principle of targeting. Contrary to the conventional pollution-haven prediction, the environmentally unconcerned country need not be the exporter of the polluting good. As country A's valuation of environmental quality increases, or country B's production-cost advantage narrows, production shifts toward A, which eventually becomes the exporter. Beyond a critical threshold, trade reduces global emissions relative to autarky. Welfare effects are asymmetric: trade always benefits country B but may either increase or decrease welfare in country A.

title:
Machine Learning-driven Crop Recommendation System for Sustainable Agriculture Under Variable Climate Conditions: 
A TabTransformer Approach using Smart Farming Sensor Data

detail.title:
Machine Learning-driven Crop Recommendation System for Sustainable Agriculture Under Variable Climate Conditions: 
A TabTransformer Approach using Smart Farming Sensor Data
detail.abstract: Agriculture in the United States is a critical economic sector, contributing over $1.3 trillion annually and supporting millions of jobs. However, challenges such as climate variability, soil degradation, and resource scarcity increasingly threaten productivity in regions like the Midwest Corn Belt and California. This paper presents a machine learning-based crop recommendation system using the TabTransformer model, a Transformer architecture tailored for tabular data, to recommend optimal crops based on soil moisture, soil pH, temperature, rainfall, humidity, sunlight hours, and normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). The system promotes sustainable farming by reducing input waste and enhancing yields. Experiments conducted on the Smart Farming Sensor Data for Yield Prediction dataset demonstrate an overall classification accuracy of 96.2% for recommending five major U.S. crops: wheat, maize, soybean, cotton, and rice. Feature analysis shows that rainfall and soil moisture are the most influential predictors. The results indicate that Transformer-based models can outperform traditional decision tree baselines while remaining computationally efficient and suitable for low-resource environments. This research contributes to the advancement of artificial intelligence in U.S. agriculture, aligning closely with USDA sustainability goals while demonstrating the potential to reduce fertilizer usage by 25-35%. The proposed system fosters sustainable farming through data-driven insights that improve resource efficiency and enhance food security.

title: Honesty, Locality and the Logarithm: Shannon's Entropy as Expected Utility
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Honesty, Locality and the Logarithm: Shannon's Entropy as Expected Utility
detail.abstract: Bernardo (1979) showed that a smooth utility function for reporting a probability density which is proper (honesty is uniquely optimal) and local (only the density ordinate at the realized value matters) must be logarithmic, u{q(•), ψ} = A log q(ψ) + B(ψ) with A > 0. We revisit this result. We make the probability spaces explicit, including the decision space of reported densities and the measure-theoretic definition of an ordinate, and give a selfcontained calculus of variations proof: a two point variation lemma establishes that the Lagrange multiplier is a universal constant, an explicit divergence construction signs A, and Gibbs' inequality supplies the converse with no smoothness at all. A parallel finite dimensional proof isolates exactly why three states are needed and why the theorem fails on two. We then relate the variational argument to Shannon (1948)'s original derivation of entropy from the grouping of choices into subsets. Both proofs regularize the same Cauchy functional equation, f (st) = f (s) + f (t), whose infinitesimal form t f ′ (t) = constant is Bernardo's Euler equation. Lindley's measure of the information in an experiment then emerges as the expected utility of any honest local scientist, and Bayes' theorem as the efficient processing rule for that utility.

title: Sorting Fact from Fiction When Reasoning Is Motivated
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business, , University of Vienna - Department of Government and University of Vienna

detail.title: Sorting Fact from Fiction When Reasoning Is Motivated
detail.abstract: We combine a simple theoretical framework with a survey experiment to investigate how individuals sort fact from fiction and update their assessments in societally important but politicized topics, such as climate change and public health. We show that cognitive ability improves news discernment and in particular, the ability to make correct assessments that contradict one’s prior issue positions. However, when we disaggregate results by topic, higher cognitive ability sometimes amplifies motivated decision-making rather than attenuating it. Our framework and findings suggest a hard–easy pattern: more complex issues elicit greater motivated reasoning; simpler ones elicit less. In addition, overconfidence reduces responsiveness to new information, contributing to the persistence of misperceptions. Higher institutional trust appears to weaken motivated reasoning, suggesting that institutional quality may play an important role in constraining opinion polarization.

title: Credit Portfolio Risk with Correlated Defaults and Losses: A Saddlepoint Approach
affiliations: University of Gothenburg - Department of Economics/Centre for Finance

detail.title: Credit Portfolio Risk with Correlated Defaults and Losses: A Saddlepoint Approach
detail.abstract: We study credit portfolio loss distributions in homogeneous models with stochastic individual losses that may be correlated with the default times. For conditionally independent intensity-based models, we consider individual losses whose conditional distributions are binomial and whose dependence on defaults is generated through the common factor driving the default probabilities. Building on explicit saddlepoint approximations for the default-count distribution, we derive computationally tractable semi-closed-form approximations for the tail distribution of the resulting credit portfolio loss. The construction extends to homogeneous factor copula models, including the one-factor Gaussian and Clayton copulas. When the individual losses are independent of the default times, the approach can also be adapted to intensity-based contagion models. For the stochastic-loss specification considered in the paper, the computational complexity of evaluating the portfolio loss tail at a given loss level is linear in the loss threshold and does not increase with the number of possible outcomes of each individual loss. We apply the resulting loss distributions to Value-at-Risk and study its time evolution under both CIR-driven default intensities and a one-factor Gaussian copula. The numerical results show that stochastic individual losses can produce substantial changes in Value-at-Risk relative to a constant-loss specification, even when the two models have the same expected individual loss.

title: From Data Signals to Strategic Foresight A Human-Centered AI Architecture for Risk-Aware and Resilient Decision Making

detail.title: From Data Signals to Strategic Foresight A Human-Centered AI Architecture for Risk-Aware and Resilient Decision Making
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate in environments characterized by large volumes of structured and unstructured data, rapid technological change, cyber threats, and strategic uncertainty. Although data analytics has progressed from descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive capabilities, analytical output alone does not guarantee effective strategic decisions. The central problem is therefore not only how organizations generate more intelligence from data, but how that intelligence is made explainable, contextualized, risk-aware, and actionable for human decision makers. This conceptual and critical literature-based article develops the Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Strategic Decision Intelligence (AI-SDI) Framework. The framework integrates data and information management, descriptive through prescriptive analytics, artificial intelligence and advanced computation, explainability and knowledge, risk and resilience, strategic decision intelligence, and human governance and action. A critical synthesis of research on analytics capabilities, AI business value, decision intelligence, explainable AI, human-AI collaboration, edge-cloud intelligence, cybersecurity, and advanced optimization identifies four persistent gaps: analytics-to-decision, prediction-to-action, AI-to-human-judgment, and performance-to-trust/resilience. The article argues that strategic decision intelligence should be designed as a socio-technical process rather than as a fully automated prediction engine. The proposed framework contributes an integrated conceptual architecture that connects analytical capability to strategic alternatives, risk-reward evaluation, managerial judgment, action, and continuous learning. The article is conceptual and does not report new experiments, datasets, statistical tests, or empirical performance results. It concludes with propositions and a research agenda for empirical validation across organizational and high-stakes decision environments.

title: Artificial Intelligence Liability and Tort Law: Causation, Foreseeability, and Legal Responsibility for Autonomous AI Harm

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Liability and Tort Law: Causation, Foreseeability, and Legal Responsibility for Autonomous AI Harm
detail.abstract: Tort doctrine allocates liability for machine-caused harm by asking what a reasonable manufacturer could have foreseen at the moment a product left its hands. That question assumes a product whose risk profile is fixed at the point of sale. Autonomous artificial intelligence systems violate this assumption: their decision-making capacities change after deployment through continued training, fine-tuning, contextual adaptation, and interaction with data the original designer never observed. This article argues that negligence and product-liability doctrine have responded to this mismatch inconsistently and, in most jurisdictions, implicitly rather than explicitly, producing causation outcomes that track litigation strategy more than the underlying epistemic reality of how these systems fail. Using a comparative doctrinal method across the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and Brazil, the article traces how the temporal reference point of foreseeability is being relocated-largely without express acknowledgment-from the moment of design to the moment of last meaningful system modification. It examines Benavides v. Tesla, Inc., the EU's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the UK's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, and Brazil's pending PL 2338/2023 as evidence of this unarticulated shift. The article's original contribution is a proposed doctrinal reconstruction-the Dynamic Foreseeability and Monitoring Standard-under which a continuing duty to monitor deployed systems generates an independent, judicially cognizable causal pathway distinct from the original design defect. The article evaluates this proposal against institutional capacity constraints, identifies its strongest doctrinal objections, and specifies the evidentiary conditions under which the standard would not apply. The author critically reviewed, edited, verified, and assumed responsibility for all legal analysis, argumentation, sources, interpretations, and conclusions contained in the final manuscript.

title: Organic Hotspots in U.S. Agriculture, 2016 to 2023, and Their Impacts on Local Economies
affiliations: College of Agricultural Sciences, Department of Agricultural Economics and Rural Sociology, College of Agricultural Sciences, Department of Agricultural Economics and Rural Sociology, Pennsylvania State University - Population Research Institute and Pennsylvania State University

detail.title: Organic Hotspots in U.S. Agriculture, 2016 to 2023, and Their Impacts on Local Economies

detail.abstract: From 2016 to 2019, a series of papers showed three important trends in U.S. organic agriculture: (a) there were prominent clusters or hotspots of certified organic operations, mostly on the West Cost, Northeast, and Upper Midwest, (b) county-level characteristics were strongly associated with the presence of an organic hotspot and, most importantly, and (c) the presence of a hotspot led to improvements in county-level indicators of economic welfare. This paper updates those papers using similar methods but newer data. Our three main findings are that (i) organic hotspots are still prominent and their positioning is largely the same as before, (ii) county-level characteristics, including some that describe the landscape of organic certifiers, are still associated with and can help predict the presence of an organic hotspot, and (iii) that counties in organic hotpots still have higher median household income and lower poverty rates than their non-organic counterparts.

title: Psychologism, Praxeology and Thymology in the Work of Ludwig von Mises: A Methodological Inquiry
affiliations: Fayetteville State University - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Psychologism, Praxeology and Thymology in the Work of Ludwig von Mises: A Methodological Inquiry
detail.abstract: This study examines the anti-psychologistic methodology of Ludwig von Mises (1881-1973), one of the most important economists of the twentieth century and a central figure of the Austrian School of Economics. Using an AI-assisted research methodology, it traces Mises's systematic effort to separate economics-understood as the a priori science of human action, or praxeology-from empirical psychology. The study identifies the key psychology-related terms in Mises's own writings, distinguishes them from vocabulary introduced by later commentators, and documents how Mises constructed a three-part methodological framework consisting of praxeology, thymology and psychology. It also examines how subsequent Austrian economists, including Murray N. Rothbard, Hans-Hermann Hoppe and Israel M. Kirzner, extended or elaborated this anti-psychologistic tradition. The findings confirm that Mises himself never used the specific term "psychologizing," which is associated primarily with Rothbard and later Austrian writers, while Mises's own vocabulary centered on the distinction between praxeology and psychology, the concept of thymology and the rejection of psychologism in epistemology. An interactive dashboard presenting the primary and secondary literature on this theme is available at https://mises-dashboard.pplx.app.

title: TetraFuse: A Synergistic Four-Dimensional Dynamic Fusion Framework for Efficient and Robust Medical Image Classification
affiliations: Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: TetraFuse: A Synergistic Four-Dimensional Dynamic Fusion Framework for Efficient and Robust Medical Image Classification
detail.abstract: Accurate medical image classification is a cornerstone of intelligent diagnostic systems; however, models must be robust to heterogeneous clinical data, sensitive to subtle pathological cues, and highly efficient for resource-constrained edge deployment. Existing lightweight networks often reduce computational cost by isolating channel groups, thereby weakening the representation of lesion features. Furthermore, they struggle to balance the suppression of shallow background noise with the preservation of deep semantic contours. To address these challenges, we propose  TetraFuse, a synergistic four-dimensional dynamic fusion framework that integrates spatial, channel, statistical, and frequency cues. Specifically, a Cross-Channel Dynamic Aggregation module reconstructs global channel topology to prevent feature isolation with negligible computational overhead. To enhance representation fidelity across layers, a Local Variance-Guided Excitation mechanism suppresses shallow background artifacts by modeling statistical heterogeneity, while a High-Frequency Boundary Injector prevents over-smoothing by preserving deep contour details. Extensive experiments on three distinct medical datasets (COVID-19, ISIC 2018, and Kvasir) demonstrate that TetraFuse achieves state-of-the-art diagnostic performance. Notably, the TetraFuse-Tiny variant reduces floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 91.5% compared to the standard ResNet50 baseline. On the Kvasir endoscopy dataset, it achieves an accuracy of 0.913 and an AUC of 0.992 with a computational cost of only 0.345G FLOPs. These results confirm that TetraFuse successfully balances rigorous diagnostic precision with operational efficiency, making it highly suitable for intelligent clinical pattern recognition systems. Our codes will be made available to facilitate research and development.

title: Cartels with a Conscience: The Case for Rule of Reason in Mixed-Motive Boycotts

detail.title: Cartels with a Conscience: The Case for Rule of Reason in Mixed-Motive Boycotts
detail.abstract:
Antitrust regulators have recently begun scrutinizing ostensibly “prosocial” coordination among economic actors including advertiser boycotts, content moderation coalitions, ESG and climate alliances, and DEI initiatives, as potential violations of § 1 of the Sherman Act. Participants in these arrangements contend that their conduct is not merely “prosocial” but also expressive of their political and ideological commitments and therefore protected by the First Amendment. These disputes raise a pressing question: when does concerted economic conduct that is also an expression of the actors’ political or ideological position receive First Amendment protection, and when does it remain subject to antitrust scrutiny? 

This Article argues that these cases constitute a distinct category of “mixed-motive” boycotts: concerted refusals to deal orchestrated by economic actors against economic actors and motivated by both commercial and noncommercial objectives. Because they are neither traditional political boycotts nor conventional economic cartels, the Supreme Court’s political boycott exemption in Claiborne Hardware does not readily extend to them. As protections for corporate speech have expanded, the boundary between political and economic boycotts has become nebulous. The Article argues that mixed-motive boycotts should not receive categorical First Amendment immunity. Extending such immunity would create an exit hatch through which sophisticated firms could evade antitrust scrutiny by recasting commercial coordination in expressive terms, thereby hollowing out the prohibition on group boycotts. The history of Noerr-Pennington demonstrates how broad First Amendment immunities can shield anticompetitive conduct. 

Instead, the Article proposes that mixed-motive boycotts should be evaluated under antitrust’s rule of reason standard. Per se treatment is ill-suited because mixed-motive boycotts encompass a heterogeneous set of practices whose competitive effects are ambiguous and may even be competition-enhancing. Some forms of coordinated conduct, such as collective efforts to improve platform safety or content moderation, may improve platform quality and increase participation rather than reduce competition. Both categorical First Amendment immunity and per se illegality are doctrinal extremes: the former overprotects speech and under-protects competition, while the latter overprotects competition and under-protects speech. The rule of reason offers a principled middle ground by requiring proof of actual competitive harm. 

Much of the recent antitrust scrutiny of prosocial coordination appears misplaced because there is little evidence that these arrangements have harmed competition in any properly defined market. That reality creates a temptation to adopt the doctrinal shortcut of conferring categorical First Amendment immunity. But hard cases make bad law. The rule of reason, though more demanding, allows courts to reach the same result without distorting § 1 doctrine or creating a new constitutional safe harbor for coordinated conduct among economic actors.

detail.abstract: Experimental evidence on diagnosis-contingent healthcare contracts shows that conditioning treatment subsidies on diagnostic verification significantly reduces medical overtreatment and corrects biased patient expectations. However, existing frameworks rely on static, binary subsidies at retail points of care. We extend this literature by formulating a dynamic, valuebased precision capitation model integrated with continuous diagnostic scoring and zero-copay digital triaging. In this paper the author proposes to model a health system that replaces fixed fee-for-service margins with risk-adjusted bundled payments tied to biomarker precision scores. The framework demonstrates that decoupling provider margins from drug utilization while offsetting patient access frictions reduces total episodic expenditures while maximizing diagnostic accuracy.

title: Natural Disasters and Household Medical Spending Risk

detail.title: Natural Disasters and Household Medical Spending Risk
detail.abstract: This paper study the distributional effects of the 2022 Sylhet floods on out-of-pocket (OOP) health expenditure in Bangladesh. Using the nationally representative 2022 Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES), identify the impact of the disaster with a difference-indifferences design that exploits district-level flood exposure and the survey's term-by-term timing. The flood had little effect on average OOP spending but reshaped the upper tail of the distribution: among households with positive health spending, exposure raised the probability of spending above the pre-flood 75th percentile by roughly 11 percentage points, with no comparable effect at lower thresholds or at the extreme top of the distribution. The flood thus did not raise health spending uniformly but concentrated additional, potentially catastrophic, costs on a subset of affected households. A decomposition of spending attributes this increase to outpatient care medicines, diagnostics, and transport rather than to hospitalization, and triple-difference estimates show that the burden fell disproportionately on the medically vulnerable, particularly households reporting chronic illness or recent illness or injury.

title: Measuring Internally Generated Intangible Capital from the Inside
affiliations: Thunderbird School of Global Management, Arizona State University

detail.title: Measuring Internally Generated Intangible Capital from the Inside
detail.abstract: I develop a firm-level measure of internally generated organization-capital investment from employee-level workforce data rather than from capitalization parameters inferred from accounting outcomes or market prices. Using 384 million employment records at U.S. public firms and O*NET task data, I distinguish labor devoted to capital building from labor supporting current operations and use it to estimate firm-level organization-capital investment. Independent accounting outcomes support the measurement without determining the occupational classification or the firm-level workforce structure. Capital-building workforce structure varies substantially and persistently among firms within the same industry, and its formation is visible in hiring around listing. Firm-level workforce information predicts subsequent capitalization out of sample and contains information about whether firms build intangible capabilities internally or acquire them.

title: Are Investors Risk Averse, Perverse or Diverse? (or Where are the Econs and KaTs?)
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Are Investors Risk Averse, Perverse or Diverse? (or Where are the Econs and KaTs?)
detail.abstract: Merriam-Webster defines "averse" as "having an active feeling of repugnance, dislike, or distaste", "perverse" as "turned away from what is right or good," and "diverse" as "differing from one another". We attempt to prove with a number of country surveys (for the US, UK, India, China and Turkiye-countries that would account for 40% of the world's population) that the fundamental assumptions of Expected Utility Theory (EUT), that investors ("Econs") are risk averse, later overturned by Prospect Theory (PT) as being (what we use poetic license to call) "perverse" (or "KaTs), missed what is reasonable to be expected; namely, investors are much more diverse. We refer to the representative investors of EUT and PT as "Econs" and "KaTs", respectively, but do not find a lot of Econs or KaTs in macro or micro analyses of these surveys. Muralidhar and Berlik (2017) demonstrated diversity within a US population at the individual level using 14 of Kahneman-Tversky's original gambles, and attempted to quantify their "Value Function." Using country surveys, and the same general approach, we show that there is diversity across countries too. At a macro level, generalizing across relatively small samples (but larger than Kahneman-Tversky's original sample size of Israeli students), developed countries appear to be risk averse, and developing countries with an Asian-bias are risk seeking. None appear to have preferences consistent with PT or EUT, but even within these classifications there is a lot of diversity. At a micro level, and using broad definitions of Econs and KaTs, we find that Econs and KaTs are very hard to find globally. These findings have interesting implications for finance theory, financial policy, design of financial products and possibly regulation.

detail.abstract:
Suriname is positioned to absorb more capital, faster, than its institutions have previously had to accommodate. The USD 10.5 billion GranMorgu development offshore Block 58 was sanctioned in October 2024 with first oil targeted for 2028, and the IMF projects mineral fiscal revenues rising from approximately USD 420 million in 2023 to a peak near USD 3.1 billion in 2033, in a country of roughly 646,000 people.

Drawing on over three months of field research in Paramaribo during 2026, this paper argues that the principal financial integrity risk is not enforcement failure but absorption capacity. Five findings are advanced. First, Suriname's absence from the FATF grey list reflects the allocation of that process rather than assessed performance: the CFATF 2023 mutual evaluation rated the jurisdiction at a low level of effectiveness across all eleven Immediate Outcomes. Second, physical infrastructure constraints translate directly into compliance constraints. Third, the near-term laundering exposure sits in artisanal gold rather than oil, where informal payment practice means there is frequently no transaction available to monitor. Fourth, the operative failure mode is correspondent banking withdrawal rather than regulatory action, in a region that lost more than forty percent of its correspondent relationships between 2011 and 2020. Fifth, the binding constraint is trained practitioner capacity rather than legislative gaps.

The paper concludes that the window to build compliance architecture alongside capital deployment, rather than retrofitting it after a correspondent relationship is terminated, closes around first oil. Observations are drawn from field research and are situated against CFATF, IMF, World Bank, FATF and INTERPOL sources.

title: Investors and Inflation
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Investors and Inflation
detail.abstract: We study how the source of inflation and the investor base jointly shape portfolio rebalancing. We distinguish between cost-push ("bad") inflation and demand-driven ("good") inflation. Using expectations from the Survey of Professional Forecasters as a proxy for sophisticated investors' beliefs, we show that bad inflation shocks induce stagflationary expectations, whereas good inflation shocks raise expected inflation and improve expected economic activity. Remarkably, household expectations move in a similar way. Using security-level holdings of bond and equity mutual fund shares, we show that portfolio rebalancing is broadly consistent with these shifts in expectations: bad inflation generates outflows from both bond and equity funds, whereas good inflation generates outflows from bond funds and inflows into equity funds. Our identification strategy compares flows across fund shares held by different investor types within the same fund, holding the underlying portfolio risk fixed. We show that the investor base determines how rebalancing unfolds: investment funds rebalance rapidly and strongly, households adjust more gradually but persistently, and insurance companies rebalance more selectively. Within bond funds, portfolios with higher residual maturity-our proxy for duration exposure-experience larger return losses following both types of inflation shocks. Residual maturity matters particularly for institutional investors: following good inflation, flows by investment funds and insurance companies are consistent with a shift from higher-to lower-maturity funds, whereas household flows vary less with maturity. Following bad inflation, investors redeem from both maturity segments. The source of inflation therefore determines the direction of portfolio rebalancing while investor composition and duration exposure determine its speed, persistence, and distribution across asset classes and maturities.

title: TRADE INTEGRATION AND INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT IN NIGERIA: ASSESSING THE IMPLICATIONS OF THE AFRICAN CONTINENTAL FREE TRADE AREA (AfCFTA)
affiliations: University of Jos,  and Nigerian Institute of Leather and Science Technology

detail.title: TRADE INTEGRATION AND INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT IN NIGERIA: ASSESSING THE IMPLICATIONS OF THE AFRICAN CONTINENTAL FREE TRADE AREA (AfCFTA)
detail.abstract: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) represents one of Africa's most ambitious economic integration initiatives, with significant implications for trade expansion, industrialization, and structural transformation. This study examines the implications of AfCFTA for trade integration and industrial development in Nigeria using a policy-oriented secondary data approach. Data were obtained from the Central Bank of Nigeria, National Bureau of Statistics, Nigerian Export Promotion Council, United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, African Union publications, and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The analysis combined descriptive statistics, comparative policy analysis, qualitative content analysis, and SWOT analysis to assess Nigeria's preparedness for AfCFTA implementation. The findings indicate gradual improvements in Nigeria's intra-African trade participation and manufacturing diversification. However, persistent challenges, including inadequate infrastructure, unreliable electricity supply, regulatory inefficiencies, limited access to finance, and weak industrial competitiveness, continue to constrain the country's ability to maximize the benefits of continental trade liberalization. The study further reveals that achieving the full industrial potential of AfCFTA requires complementary domestic reforms aimed at strengthening productive capacity, improving the business environment, deepening regional value-chain integration, and enhancing institutional coordination. By jointly assessing trade performance, industrial readiness, and policy capacity, the study provides a comprehensive policy perspective to support strategic industrial development and Nigeria's effective participation in the AfCFTA framework.

title: Conditionally Stable Motivation: A Neurocomputational Model of Long-Horizon Goal Persistence under Extreme Reward Sparsity

detail.title: Conditionally Stable Motivation: A Neurocomputational Model of Long-Horizon Goal Persistence under Extreme Reward Sparsity
detail.abstract: Long-horizon human pursuits (e.g., lifelong projects, scientific careers, entrepreneurship, elite training) sometimes show a striking pattern: persistence with low or zero immediate reward for extended periods, punctuated by sudden, intense bursts of goal-directed activity when opportunities arise. Classical reinforcement learning (RL) and canonical motivational theories-which emphasize reward prediction errors, temporal discounting, and reward-driven value updating-struggle to capture this enduring yet conditional persistence. Here we formalize and defend a neurocomputational hypothesis we call Conditionally Stable Motivation (CSM). CSM posits that (i) certain high-order goals are encoded as stable latent value attractors (state components, not ephemeral reward signals), (ii) a latent opportunity set mediates whether the goal s motivational potential remains active, and (iii) neural circuits implement a two-mode control policy (maintenance vs. exploitation) governed by the opportunity set, with dopaminergic signals acting primarily as opportunity indicators rather than pure reward prediction errors in this regime. We present a precise mathematical model (state augmentation, motivational potential, policy switching rules), map model components to plausible neural substrates (vmPFC, dlPFC, ACC, ventral striatum/VTA), derive empirical predictions, and outline experiments and simulation paradigms for validation. We argue that CSM (a) reconciles long-horizon persistence with sparse rewards, (b) makes falsifiable neurophysiological predictions distinct from standard RL, and (c) provides a framework for understanding both adaptive persistence and pathological forms of unyielding pursuit.

title: Instrument Hacking
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School, UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics and University of New South Wales

detail.title: Instrument Hacking
detail.abstract:
In instrumental-variable (IV) studies, researchers often evaluate multiple candidate instruments and selectively report the specification with the most favorable first- or second-stage statistics. We show that this form of instrument selection (“instrument-hacking”) induces median bias in IV estimators toward the OLS estimand, undermining the rationale for using IV. When all candidate instruments have the same true strength, median bias increases monotonically with the number of available instruments. More generally, when candidate instruments differ in true strength, monotonicity need not hold because increasing the number of instruments can lead researchers to select genuinely stronger instruments. Nonetheless, in simulations calibrated to the empirical distribution of instrument strengths in the IV literature, median bias increases monotonically with the number of available instruments. Furthermore, it is substantial in magnitude, even when only a few instruments are available.

title: The Yeoman's Portfolio: Measuring Historical Risk Preferences Using Crop Choice
affiliations: University of Connecticut and University of Connecticut

detail.title: The Yeoman's Portfolio: Measuring Historical Risk Preferences Using Crop Choice
detail.abstract:
We design a method for measuring the risk preferences of agents in the deep past. The method combines a structural model of crop choice as a portfolio allocation with machine-learning prediction of expected crop returns, using historic agronomic and climate data. We estimate county-level risk preferences for the United States and farmer-level preferences in Kansas from 1889 to 1929. More risk averse farmers leveraged less, were less likely to purchase novel WWI Liberty Bonds, and were more likely to participate in local risk-sharing institutions. We show that higher risk aversion predicts slower tractor adoption and farm mechanization during the 1920s.

title: Occupational Licensing of Uber Drivers
affiliations: , University of Victoria, Humphrey School of Public Affairs and University of Nevada, Reno

detail.title: Occupational Licensing of Uber Drivers
detail.abstract:
We examine whether occupational licensing improves service quality and safety using trip-level Uber data that include driver ratings and telematics-based measures of driving behavior. Exploiting quasi-random assignment from proximity-based dispatch, we compare trips served by licensed and unlicensed drivers in two settings: a cross-border comparison between New York City and New Jersey, and a deregulation event in Houston. Across settings and specifications, including instrumental variable estimates, we find no consistent evidence that licensing improves consumer outcomes. In Houston, post-deregulation entrants are indistinguishable from previously licensed drivers on ratings and driving behavior, despite differing markedly in experience and age.

title: Political Entrepreneurs
affiliations: Duke University, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Duke University and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Political Entrepreneurs
detail.abstract:
Firms shape public policy not only from the outside through lobbying and campaign contributions, but also from the inside when business owners hold public office. We study this channel using a novel dataset that links state legislators’ personal financial disclosures to bill sponsorship records across 26 U.S. states from 2009 to 2023. The disclosures allow us to observe business ownership during legislative service and to distinguish entrepreneurs, defined as legislators who both own and actively manage a firm, from passive shareholders and employees. Applying a large language model to bill text, we classify legislation as pro-business and identify a subset of pro-entry bills that reduce barriers facing new firms. Entrepreneurs are a substantial presence in state legislatures, accounting for over 40 percent of legislators, and their representation varies primarily across states rather than within states over time. Although entrepreneurs do not sponsor more bills overall, they initiate a greater share of bills as first or sole primary sponsor. They also do not appear to be generic advocates for business. Relative to legislators with other business ties, entrepreneurs are no more likely to sponsor pro-business bills or bills endorsed by state Chambers of Commerce. Instead, they selectively advance pro-entry legislation, especially bills related to deregulation and innovation rather than antitrust or access to capital. These findings document an important channel through which entrepreneurs shape the policy environment for entrepreneurship from within political institutions.

title: Rate Risk and Rate Insurance
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Rate Risk and Rate Insurance
detail.abstract:
I decompose stock returns into a duration-matched Treasury component, identified from monetary policy surprises, and a payoff component. Risk and returns rise much less with duration for stocks than for their matched Treasuries. Stock volatility is dampened by rate insurance: rates fall in bad times, so the bond inside a stock provides insurance against the stock’s payoff risk. Expected stock returns are dampened because the insurance works in reverse: rates rise in good times, so stocks’ payoff gains hedge the losses borne by investors holding net duration, notably government bonds when Ricardian equivalence fails. This framework helps reconcile positive bond premia with negative stock-bond covariance, sheds light on equity anomalies and the collapse of the value premium, implies that fiscal and monetary policy shape bond and equity premia, and motivates a two-factor model that jointly prices stocks and bonds. Rate insurance can even turn the price of long-run risk negative, explaining why long bonds beat long stocks.

title: Local Labor Demand and Achievement Gaps: Evidence from the Great Recession
affiliations: Pomona College and Claremont McKenna College

detail.title: Local Labor Demand and Achievement Gaps: Evidence from the Great Recession
detail.abstract:
We examine how contractions in local labor demand during the Great Recession affected children's academic achievement. We combine county-level test scores for grades 3–8 from the Stanford Education Data Archive with a shift-share design that interacts counties' 2005 industry composition with national industry employment growth, isolating demand-driven changes in local employment. Following recent advances in the shift-share literature, we validate the design with balance, pre-trend, and Rotemberg-weight diagnostics and report exposure-robust standard errors throughout. A one-standard-deviation adverse shock lowers mathematics achievement by about 0.03 student-level standard deviations and widens the White–Black and economic-disadvantage achievement gaps in both subjects. Within a common geography, losses concentrate among economically disadvantaged students. English language arts estimates point in the same direction but are harder to separate from the Great Recession's housing bust, and we interpret them as the combined effect of the labor-demand contraction and the associated decline in house prices. The achievement response is concentrated in the recession window. The post-2014 period, identified mainly by the oil-price cycle, yields a precise null, so our estimates measure the response to severe contractions rather than a general business-cycle parameter. School funding did not respond contemporaneously to these shocks, while family income, child poverty, and house prices all did.

title: Labor Market Power with Worker and Firm Heterogeneity
affiliations: Duke University, Fuqua School of Business-Economics Group, University of Minnesota - Minneapolis, Duke University and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis

detail.title: Labor Market Power with Worker and Firm Heterogeneity
detail.abstract:
How do firms set wages? How should governments set income taxes? If labor supply is inelastic to wages, firms can pay workers less than their marginal products, and governments can increase taxes without eroding the base. However, the structure of labor supply elasticities in the economy is complex. Recent empirics document variation across workers, firms, and margins (which firm to work at versus how many hours to work). To account for this rich structure of labor supply elasticities we extend the neoclassical model to include a discrete choice over which firm to work at, production complementarities and strategic interaction between heterogeneous, granular firms. In terms of wage setting, we find that novel effects of worker heterogeneity account for 78 percent of the variable component of labor supply elasticities and markdowns, and 89 percent of markdown differences between large and small firms. In terms of policy, higher progressivity makes labor supply less elastic, eroding the tax base by widening markdowns and worsening sorting. These channels (i) produce large declines in earnings following increases in marginal tax rates, consistent with empirical studies, and (ii) reduce optimal tax progressivity by one-third and associated welfare gains by two-thirds.

title: Tracing the Impact of Payment Convenience on Deposits: Evidence from Depositor Activeness
affiliations: , University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business and

detail.title: Tracing the Impact of Payment Convenience on Deposits: Evidence from Depositor Activeness
detail.abstract:
How slow are bank transfers, and how do transfer delays affect deposit demand? Using transaction-level data from millions of depositors, we measure transfer delays by matching debits and credits across accounts held by the same depositor. Shorter delays correlate with more transfers and lower balances. Exploiting county-level exposure to Zelle’s staggered rollout, we find that faster payments reduce delays and deposit growth. Calibrating a deposit-management model, we find that transfer delays raise deposit demand, and the magnitude of this effect varies with interest rates and consumption volatility. Payment frictions therefore shape transactional deposit demand and monetary transmission.

title: Benchmark Mineability and the Financing of AI Innovation
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Benchmark Mineability and the Financing of AI Innovation
detail.abstract:
Public AI benchmarks steer research and allocate investments. They are therefore market designs. Public examples can reveal the process behind a private final test, while a finite public score cannot cover a broad task space inherent to general intelligence. I show how both gaps become profitable when scores move capital and how targeted effort erodes the signal used by later investors. The market design lesson is to separate development from certification: publish practice tasks, but choose the investment-consequential generator after the submitted system's evaluation policy is fixed.

title: Monetary-Fiscal Interactions: A Reappraisal
affiliations: Northwestern University, University of California, Berkeley, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Northwestern University

detail.title: Monetary-Fiscal Interactions: A Reappraisal
detail.abstract:
The possibility of fiscal dominance in the representative-agent New Keynesian model (RANK) hinges on the assumption that income is perpetually demand-determined: fiscal deficits can drive output and inflation within that model only insofar as they trigger infinitely lasting, self-sustained shifts in aggregate spending and income. Moving to heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian models (HANK) opens the door to a different pathway: classical non-Ricardian effects, due to finite horizons or liquidity constraints. A refinement motivated by the model's intended focus on short-run phenomena—requiring a return to flexible-price outcomes in finite time—arrests the infinite feedback loop between spending and income, leaving only the classical non-Ricardian mechanism, and makes sure that the study of monetary-fiscal interactions is not centered on hard-to-test assumptions regarding beliefs at infinity.

title: Beyond The Triffin Dilemma: Restructuring Sovereign Debt Dynamics Via Closed-Loop Dollar Velocity and High-Value Export Re-Absorption

detail.title: Beyond The Triffin Dilemma: Restructuring Sovereign Debt Dynamics Via Closed-Loop Dollar Velocity and High-Value Export Re-Absorption

detail.abstract: This research paper develops a macroeconomic framework to resolve the foundational paradox of the global reserve currency system-formalized by the Triffin Dilemma. Under the modern international monetary architecture, the reserve-issuing sovereign is structurally compelled to run chronic current account deficits to supply cross-border liquidity, accelerating sovereign liability accumulation and compounding long-term currency debasement pressures. We propose a macroeconomic model establishing that sovereign debt expansion can be decoupled from systemic currency debasement and stagflationary pressures. By implementing a Closed-Loop Dollar Velocity Framework, global reserve holdings are systematically vectorized and absorbed into high-margin domestic capital goods, artificial intelligence architectures, advanced technological infrastructure, specialized intellectual property (𝐼𝑃), and sovereign bio-agricultural commodities and food-security assets (𝐴𝑔𝑇𝑒𝑐ℎ). Using endogenous growth specifications, we demonstrate that routing foreign capital claims through a closed export-import circuit elevates Total Factor Productivity (𝑇𝐹𝑃), rebalances the Balance of Payments (𝐵𝑜𝑃), endogenously attenuates long-term interest rates (𝑟 ↓), yields an indicative scenario projection of approximately 2 to 3 million net high-skill domestic jobs over a 36-month horizon, and stabilizes the national debt-to-GDP trajectory without domestic fiscal austerity or global liquidity contraction.

title: Disclosure Stops Before Resilience: Public Evidence on AI Dependencies at Global Systemically Important Banks

detail.title: Disclosure Stops Before Resilience: Public Evidence on AI Dependencies at Global Systemically Important Banks
detail.abstract: This study examines how far public information allows external observers to move from a bank's visible artificial-intelligence (AI) use to disclosure relevant to dependency resilience. We audit all 29 banks on the Financial Stability Board's 2025 G-SIB list using a frozen twocorpus protocol. The bank, not an individual service path, is the unit of analysis. The eightelement sequence covers AI materiality, concrete use, external-stack visibility, AI-specific risk, linked dependency, common dependency, substitutability, and tested resilience. Under the strict AI-specific rule, 23 banks reach AI-risk recognition, seven reach linked dependency, and three reach common dependency; under the broader enabling-technology rule, 22 reach dependency and six reach common dependency. No bank completes either sequence through tested resilience. Two blinded independent model recodings agree on 87.4% of 348 institution-item decisions (pooled Cohen's kappa = 0.719; Gwet's AC1 = 0.771), and both independently end at zero complete tested sequences despite different intermediate counts. The evidence concerns public assessability within the specified corpus, not internal control quality or a verified service-level dependency path. The study identifies a bank-level linkage gap and proposes separate minimum disclosures for public comparability and confidential supervisory collection.

title: Beyond Participation: Explaining Productivity and Income Outcomes in Nigeria's Rice Value Chain Development Programme
affiliations: Henan University

detail.title: Beyond Participation: Explaining Productivity and Income Outcomes in Nigeria's Rice Value Chain Development Programme

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Participation in the study was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from participants before data collection. Participants were informed of the purpose of the study and that their responses would be used for research purposes.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding

detail.abstract: For smallholder rice farmers, higher farm productivity does not necessarily translate into higher household income. This paper examines this gap using evidence from the IFAD-supported Value Chain Development Programme (VCDP) among rice farmers in Niger, Taraba, and Benue States, Nigeria. Primary survey data from 282 farmers are combined with five key-informant interviews and four focus group discussions. Logistic regression is used to examine programme participation, OLS models estimate the conditional associations of programme participation and training with post-programme rice productivity, and Firth logistic models examine reported household-income improvement. Programme participation is positively associated with post-programme rice productivity, corresponding to approximately 11.7% higher predicted yield, although the association is only marginally significant. Training has a larger and statistically significant association with productivity, corresponding to approximately 35.8% higher predicted yield among trained farmers. Neither programme participation nor training is significantly associated with reported household-income improvement, and their interaction is also insignificant. The financial-constraint index is negatively associated with participation, productivity, and income improvement. The findings indicate that programme participation alone does not capture the productive differences associated with value-chain support. Training is more closely associated with productivity, while financial and production constraints remain associated with weaker outcomes. The findings also show that farm-level productivity gains cannot be assumed to translate into equivalent household-income gains.

title: What Ties Us Together? Explaining Synchronized GDP Volatility
affiliations: Universidad de Alicante, University of Granada and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: What Ties Us Together? Explaining Synchronized GDP Volatility
detail.abstract: Amid heightened policy uncertainty, understanding the drivers of global macroeconomic instability becomes increasingly critical. This paper studies the determinants of output volatility synchronization using data for 42 economies worldwide. We construct a bilateral time-varying index of volatility synchronization and infer its drivers using Bayesian model averaging, complemented by weighted average least squares (WALS) and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. We find that differences in total factor productivity, interest rate, and fiscal policy volatility robustly explain crosscountry synchronization, with nuances between developed and developing countries. Overall, the results highlight the role of technological divergence and macroeconomic policy uncertainty in shaping the international comovement of output volatility.

title: From Narrative Scores to Phase-State-Space Market Intelligence Evidence for a Composable Measurement Layer in U.S. Equities

detail.title: From Narrative Scores to Phase-State-Space Market Intelligence Evidence for a Composable Measurement Layer in U.S. Equities
detail.abstract:
Most financial text systems compress information into sentiment or a directional score. This paper studies a different object: a proprietary measurement layer that represents each security as a moving coordinate in a narrative/evidence state space. We call the approach Phase-State-Space Market Intelligence (PSSMI). The central claim is deliberately narrower than 'AI predicts stocks': state coordinates can measure future movement intensity, directional credibility, lifecycle position, and transition dynamics; downstream investors can then combine, gate, neutralize, or transform those coordinates inside their own models. Specific estimators, thresholds, source weights, signal formulas, and execution parameters are withheld.
On a proprietary U.S.-equity panel, three core state-intensity coordinates show cross-sectional information coefficients of roughly 0.04–0.11 against subsequent absolute returns. A pre-registered magnitude composite constructed from the core coordinates produces ICs of 0.117–0.128 over 1–10 trading days with Newey-West HAC t-statistics of 10.5–12.8; the same composite has approximately zero IC against signed returns, an explicit falsification result. Top-minus-bottom decile movement spreads reach 1.9–3.3 percentage points at ten days with day-clustered t-statistics of 9.2–15.7. Level-by-change tests further show that identical high state levels behave differently depending on trajectory, supporting a phase-state rather than static-score interpretation.
We then separate measurement validity from monetization. Fixed registry rules applied to stored point-in-time scores generate several large-sample profitable signal families. A deliberately adverse T+1 next-day-close stress test preserves positive net economics in multiple core signals: selected day-clustered t-statistics range from 2.87 to 4.45, four signals survive Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery control at q≤0.05, and Hansen’s consistent Superior Predictive Ability p-value is 0.0275. Separately, the current valid-only PIT-era paper book contains 936 audited trades, a 52.7% win rate, +0.419% average net return per trade, profit factor 1.52, day-clustered t=3.04, two-way t=3.43, and HAC t=2.89.
The paper also reports negative findings. A strict frozen PIT OOS test shows that naively adding the entire narrative-state family to a strong conventional magnitude model reduces OOS IC, and the broad directional family does not yet establish strict PIT incremental alpha. These failures motivate the main interpretation: PSSMI is not a flat factor library and should not be evaluated by indiscriminate linear stacking. The evidence instead points to sparse, target-specific, regime-conditional transformations of a latent state representation. We conclude with an institutional replication roadmap designed to test that proposition without disclosing the proprietary recipe.

title: Beat the Machine: Human Judgment as a Decision Guardrail Against AI Convergence in Non-Deterministic Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Beat the Machine: Human Judgment as a Decision Guardrail Against AI Convergence in Non-Deterministic Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper is the second working paper in the Do The Right Math / DTRM Research Lab program and is designed as a direct evolution of the March 2026 SSRN paper From Game-Theoretic Decision Training to Human-in-the-Loop Event-Driven Investing. Paper I established a real-field portfolio laboratory in U.S. equities and reported five completed cohorts in which the DTRM Fund produced a published cumulative return of 32.99%, compared with 9.17% for a prompt-driven ChatGPT Fund, 8.75% for the S&P 500, and 5.98% for the AI-managed AIEQ peer. Subsequent public proof-of-work snapshots extended the program beyond the initial five cohorts: the one-year milestone reported +41.42% and second place among 11 tracked assets/benchmarks, while the August 2026 DTRM roadmap recorded +39.57%, second place, and seven live research cohorts. By the date of this manuscript, the program had progressed beyond the original seven-cohort roadmap, but only sourced snapshots are quantified here.
The present paper narrows the scientific question. Rather than asking whether a new machine predictor can replace the original deterministic XGBoost ranking, Phase 2 asks whether calibrated probabilistic downside information can constrain that ranking and improve decisions under a human-defined, frozen rule. Three quantile models (P10, P50 and P90) were calibrated on frozen validation data. Direct probabilistic ranking failed to improve the deterministic baseline (V0), and an absolute P10 > 0 veto proved infeasible out of sample with zero passers (V1). A relative downside veto, frozen before outcome inspection, then produced positive incremental Top-K mean excess-beta target in three separate temporal tests: +0.1443 in V2, +0.1494 in a prospective replication V3, and +0.0276 in the substantially longer V4 cohort. News-event cluster bootstrap 95% intervals remained above zero in all three cohorts. Ticker-cluster sensitivity was materially wider and included zero in V2 and V4, while remaining positive in V3. Within V4, four of six ISO weeks had positive incremental Top-K mean. 
The evidence therefore supports a narrower proposition than “humans always beat AI” or “the strategy is profitable.” A frozen probabilistic downside guardrail can add reproducible decision value around a deterministic machine ranking, but the magnitude is regime-dependent and not uniformly robust to cross-sectional ticker concentration. The broader DTRM “Resistance” thesis is consequently treated as a falsifiable research program: as machine systems become more capable, their shared data, objectives and architectures may also create correlated failure modes; human value may survive not by calculating the same game better, but by defining a different game, different constraints and different models of error. Financial markets remain the laboratory because they are adaptive, adversarial and non deterministic, making them a demanding environment in which to test human-AI complementarity.

title: The Inference Problem in Financial AI: Forecasting, Portfolios, Market Quality, and Systemic Resilience

detail.title: The Inference Problem in Financial AI: Forecasting, Portfolios, Market Quality, and Systemic Resilience
detail.abstract: Financial AI is commonly evaluated at the model or forecasting level, while its economically consequential effects arise through portfolio construction, market interaction, and stress-state behavior. Evidence at these layers is not interchangeable. This paper develops a cross-layer inference framework that separates five economic objects-AI capability, volatility forecasting, portfolio performance, market quality, and systemic resilience-and treats each transition as a distinct empirical question. Recent evidence reveals three recurring divergences: greater general model capability does not guarantee superior volatility forecasts; attractive AIgenerated portfolios can arise without superior forecast skill; and lower price variation can coexist with deteriorating liquidity. The framework shows why these divergences are economically meaningful rather than merely terminological: optimization can alter the value of forecasts, aggregation can transform private decisions into market-wide order flow, and liquidity or funding constraints can change normal-market relationships under stress. A structured evidence audit further reveals an identification gradient, with comparatively dense predictive evidence and much thinner evidence linking adaptive AI to systemic outcomes during real market stress. The paper does not presume that AI is stabilizing or destabilizing. It specifies where inference stops and what additional evidence is required before an upstream performance gain can support a downstream financial conclusion.

title: Lobbying as Auditing
affiliations: University of Chicago

detail.title: Lobbying as Auditing
detail.abstract: Firms hire third parties, lobbyists, to observe politicians' otherwise private efforts on the firm's behalf. Lobbyists can thereby discipline politicians, but the same relationships that facilitate monitoring create opportunities for collusion at the expense of the firm. I develop a principal-agent model of this tension. In equilibrium, monitoring disciplines the politician only when collusion risk is intermediate-a perquisite zone. When collusion is rare, monitoring costs drive the politician to reject the firm's offers. When collusion risk is high, lobbyists' reports become too unreliable to deter shirking. When lobbyists perform this monitoring role, they act like auditors on behalf of interest groups. Firms that seek behind-the-scenes political work face a counterintuitive incentive to tolerate rather than eliminate lobbyist capture to ensure that politicians find the prospect of a deal under monitoring acceptable.

title: Beyond The Lineage Myth: Dismantling Intergenerational Determinism to Enhance Entrepreneurial Intent in South Africa

detail.title: Beyond The Lineage Myth: Dismantling Intergenerational Determinism to Enhance Entrepreneurial Intent in South Africa
detail.abstract: A pervasive socio-psychological barrier in emerging markets is the belief that entrepreneurship is an inherited family asset rather than an acquired professional discipline. This paper critically deconstructs this "lineage myth," arguing that intergenerational determinism severely limits entrepreneurial intent among individuals from non-business backgrounds. Combining cognitive psychology with strategic management literature and preliminary qualitative case evidence, the study evaluates the psychological phenomenon of learned helplessness among aspiring South African founders who believe they lack the inherited capital or institutional networks necessary to scale a firm. The paper introduces the "Acquired Agency Framework," which positions entrepreneurship as a systematic, teachable capability independent of family lineage. Four preliminary cases of South African women entrepreneurs are presented to demonstrate the framework in practice. The study concludes with policy recommendations for shifting localized entrepreneurship education from basic compliance literacy to psychological empowerment and self-efficacy cultivation.

title: Balancing Innovation and Public Interest in Intellectual Property Rights: A Statutory, Economic, And Policy Analysis

detail.title: Balancing Innovation and Public Interest in Intellectual Property Rights: A Statutory, Economic, And Policy Analysis
detail.abstract: Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) represent statutory exclusive privileges conferred upon creators and inventors to catalyze capital investment in research, technological innovation, and artistic production. However, conferring unchecked market exclusivity creates severe structural friction with fundamental public welfare imperatives, including access to affordable life-saving medicines, higher education, agricultural seed sovereignty, and digital technology diffusion. This research article critically investigates the statutory, economic, and jurisprudential mechanisms designed to balance proprietary innovation with public interest safeguards under international multilateral treaties and Indian domestic law. Analyzing the TRIPS Agreement, Sections 3(d) and 84 of the Indian Patents Act, 1970, Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957, the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001, and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), this study evaluates landmark judicial decisions including Novartis v. UOI, Bayer v. Natco, the DU Photocopy Case, and Roche v. Cipla. Crucially, the author proposes a forward-looking policy framework incorporating Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) delinkage models, statutory tiered pricing, FRAND licensing for Generative AI, and emergency greenchannel compulsory licensing to reconcile dynamic innovation incentives with static welfare access.

title: AI-Enabled Strategic Decision Intelligence for Scope 1–3 Greenhouse Gas Data Quality: A Domain-Informed Autoencoder Approach

detail.title: AI-Enabled Strategic Decision Intelligence for Scope 1–3 Greenhouse Gas Data Quality: A Domain-Informed Autoencoder Approach
detail.abstract: Reliable Scope 1-3 greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories depend on heterogeneous activity data, emission factors, organizational attributes, and reported totals that are vulnerable to unit, sign, decimal, aggregation, and outlier errors. Conventional validation rules are necessary but may not scale across large inventories or reveal multivariate inconsistencies. This study develops and evaluates an AI-enabled decision-intelligence workflow that combines an unsupervised autoencoder with GHG-accounting features and a human review queue. A reproducible synthetic panel of 7,200 monthly records for 200 facilities was created, and 360 controlled anomalies were injected across five error types. Models were trained only on normal records; performance was compared with an Isolation Forest baseline on a 1,728-record test set. The domaininformed autoencoder achieved 99.5% accuracy, 97.8% precision, 100% recall, a 98.9% F1 score, and 1.000 ROC-AUC, with 360 true positives, eight false positives, and no false negatives. Isolation Forest achieved 79.0% accuracy and 2.2% recall at the selected validation-based threshold despite a 0.910 ROC-AUC, illustrating the difference between ranking ability and an operational decision rule. The contribution is not a claim of field-ready generalization; it is a transparent proof of concept showing how domain ratios, anomaly scoring, priority assignment, and human verification can convert analytics into auditable GHG data-quality action. External validation on real inventories remains essential.

title: What Do Replicability and Robustness Reveal About True Effects?
affiliations: University of Innsbruck, Stockholm School of Economics - Department of Economics and University of Innsbruck - Department of Economics

detail.title: What Do Replicability and Robustness Reveal About True Effects?
detail.abstract: How credible are published scientific findings? This question has been examined in large-scale studies testing whether original findings hold up in the original data (robustness) and in new data (replicability). However, how robustness and replicability relate to each other-and to true effect sizes-remains unclear. We use simulations to study three mechanisms that inflate published effect sizes, all rooted in selection on statistical significance: the sampling winner's curse (samples that overestimate the effect by chance are more likely to yield significance), the heterogeneity-induced winner's curse (defensible analytical choices that happen to amplify the estimate are more likely to yield significance), and p-hacking (analysts search across analyses until the result yields p < 0.05). Robustness tests can, at best, correct for heterogeneity-induced inflation and p-hacking, leaving a potentially dominant source of inflation unaddressed. Consequently, robustness effect sizes exceed true relative effect sizes by about 40 percentage points across several scenarios, and by 62-100 percentage points for false-positive findings; in many scenarios, the original p-value is about as informative about true effects as the robustness indicators. Replication studies are more informative. When analytical heterogeneity is present, conceptual replications-applying an alternative analysis to new data-are preferable to direct replications, which inherit the original analysis's heterogeneity-induced winner's curse. Conceptual replications yield unbiased estimates of true effect sizes across all scenarios studied. Multiverse replications, combining new data with multiple analyses, are the most informative design we examine.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces ordinal complementarity: a feature of stochastic production functions that is robust to monotonic transformations of inputs X and output Y. It has two equivalent definitions: supermodularity of the conditional survival function under a first-order stochastic dominance ordering, and supermodularity of E[Q(Y)|X] for all non-decreasing valuations Q. Relative to existing conventions, this definition offers a strengthening with more robust policy implications. Ordinal complementarity is necessary and sufficient for a number of social planner problems to have monotone solutions for all Q, including those with arbitrarily strong redistributive preferences. It is also testable-along with a number of related but weaker production properties-because it can be represented as a set of moment inequalities. An empirical application to the technology of cognitive skill formation for children finds different combinations of these properties at different ages, leading to new insights.
