title: Injunctions and Venture Capital: An Empirical Look at eBay's Effect on Startups
affiliations: Santa Clara University and Santa Clara University - School of Law

detail.title: Injunctions and Venture Capital: An Empirical Look at eBay's Effect on Startups

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Journal of Intellectual Property & Entertainment Law, Vol. 16, forthcoming 2027

detail.abstract: In the two decades that have passed since the Supreme Court raised the bar for awarding injunctive relief in eBay v. MercExchange, numerous descriptive studies have documented a corresponding reduction in the frequency with which patent enforcers obtain injunctions against ongoing infringement. However, surprisingly few attempts have been made to assess whether eBay had a broader effect on incentives to innovate. As a result, it remains controversial whether eBay advances patent law's fundamental goal of spurring invention--and thus should be preserved--or instead stands in the way of progress--and thus should be reversed or legislatively abrogated. We inform this active policy debate by presenting the results of an empirical analysis of eBay's effect on venture-backed startups, a segment of the innovation economy that is generally regarded as both disproportionately affected by patent protection at the margin and disproportionately responsible for economic growth and job creation. Our results suggest that eBay had a modest and mixed effect on startup performance, not the broadly negative effect predicted by critics of the decision. This is true even among medical technology startups, a group that theory predicts is especially susceptible to eBay's hypothesized harms.

title: Data-Driven Cybersecurity Decision-Making: Transforming Security Data into Strategic Intelligence

detail.title: Data-Driven Cybersecurity Decision-Making: Transforming Security Data into Strategic Intelligence
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly possess abundant cybersecurity data but still struggle to convert that data into strategic decisions. Security telemetry, cyber-threat intelligence, business information, and external signals are frequently processed through separate analytical and managerial systems, creating gaps between detection, interpretation, risk assessment, and action. This conceptual article asks how organizations can transform heterogeneous cybersecurity data into explainable, risk-aware, resilient, and human-governed strategic intelligence. Drawing on research in data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), decision intelligence, knowledge-based systems, edge-cloud computing, explainable AI (XAI), cyber resilience, human-AI collaboration, and advanced optimization, the article proposes the Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Strategic Decision Intelligence (AI-SDI) Framework. The framework contains seven layers: data and information management; analytics; AI and advanced computation; explainability and knowledge; risk and resilience; strategic decision intelligence; and human governance and action. A continuous feedback loop connects decision outcomes to new data and model or knowledge updates. The literature synthesis identifies four persistent gaps: analytics-to-decision, prediction-to-action, AI-to-humanjudgment, and performance-to-trust/resilience. Cross-domain illustrations in project portfolio management, UAV mission planning, GPS-denied autonomous systems, and enterprise cybersecurity demonstrate conceptual portability without claiming new empirical results. Six propositions are developed for future testing. The article argues that the value of data analytics is determined not by data volume, but by the quality, transparency, resilience, and accountability of the decisions it enables.

title: Make It Make Cents: How Defamation's Economic Filter Abandons the Disability Class

detail.title: Make It Make Cents: How Defamation's Economic Filter Abandons the Disability Class
detail.abstract:
American defamation converts a dignitary injury into a property injury, and the conversion decides who has a remedy. Two filters run in sequence: whether the statement was of and concerning an ascertainable plaintiff, which eliminates statements aimed at classes, and whether the plaintiff can locate the injury on a ledger. Disparagement of a disability is definitionally class directed, since nobody asserts that a named individual lacks a diagnosis; the assertion is that the category itself is fictitious. The first filter therefore extinguishes the claim before the second is reached, and where a plaintiff clears the first, the second sorts claimants by whether they sell the identity rather than by whether they were injured. The advocate who earns a living speaking about a condition can plead injury to trade or business; the worker who merely has it cannot. 
      Three corrections follow from the sources. The decision universally cited for the size rule is two opinions, and neither holds what it is said to hold. The modern test is qualitative, asking the intensity of suspicion cast upon the plaintiff, and it has permitted suit by one of sixty football players while barring one of twelve parking operators. The economic filter reaches written defamation notwithstanding a jurisdictional split over libel per quod, because the constitutional actual injury requirement runs across both from above. And the Americans with Disabilities Act already forbids the inference the disparagement rests on: substantial limitation is assessed without regard to learned adaptive modifications, and coverage extends to a person regarded as impaired whether or not any limitation exists. 
      The Article then reaches the empirical premise underneath the size rule, stated on the face of the controlling authority: that no reasonable reader draws an inference about any individual from a statement about a large class. The research on generic language contradicts it, including the work most skeptical of that literature, which finds that hearing a property predicated of a novel category leads adult listeners to attribute it to an unencountered member. This Article proposes no group libel regime and takes no side in that debate. Its claim is internal. A remedy that scales inversely with the size of the injured class leaves the widest harms with the fewest doors; hostile environment doctrine reaches class directed statements only inside a covered relationship; and a system capable of delivering an identical class disparagement to millions of individual recipients now sits precisely in the gap.

title: The Ransom Cap: Collective Commitment and the Price of Redemption *
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Government

detail.title: The Ransom Cap: Collective Commitment and the Price of Redemption *
detail.abstract: A community will pay to free its own, beyond what any market would bear. The Mishnah forbids it: captives are not redeemed above their value, mipnei tikkun ha-olam. We read the rule as a takkanah: a community binding itself against its members' mercy. We ask which externality it corrects. The Talmud names two: the drain on the common purse, and that ransoms invite further captures. We show that a cap, not a ban and not free redemption, is optimal. Its comparative statics turn on the scarcity of the purse and the responsiveness of captors. Its limit case, a self-redeemer, identifies which externality binds, and a recorded medieval dispute settles which. With a strategic captor holding a slave-market option, the cap falls on the captive's value: redemption clears, but funds no further abduction. Where a captive can be sold the cap holds; where he cannot, refusal is right.

detail.abstract: The grammar of graphics distinguishes between mapping a variable to a visual property and setting that property to a constant. The distinction is coherent, and it is where beginners get lost: both are written inside the same function call, and the wrong choice produces a figure rather than an error. This report describes a browser-based simulator that makes the distinction structural, dividing its sidebar into the four places a setting can be written and updating the figure and the code together, line by line. The tool is then used on data deposited with a published study of supplementary physics courses that the course it belongs to has already read. Plotting those data reproduces the study's regression results and adds three things the tables do not carry: how far apart the groups were before instruction, how much of an apparent association a fitted line supplies, and how one control variable is compressed against its ceiling. Each is a lesson a regression course needs and cannot easily manufacture.

title: Beneath the Trees: Natural Capital, Scarcity, and the Social Cost of Carbon under Uncertainty
affiliations: , University of Oxford, affiliation not provided to SSRN and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: Beneath the Trees: Natural Capital, Scarcity, and the Social Cost of Carbon under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: How should carbon be priced when climate change damages heterogeneous productive assets? We show that the social cost of carbon is not determined by aggregate physical damages alone. With imperfect substitution among natural-capital and other productive inputs, it depends on which inputs are damaged, how climate change alters their relative scarcity, and in which aggregate states those losses occur. We derive an exact representation of the social cost of carbon as the discounted, state-contingent value of scarcity-weighted input losses, and discipline the relevant input-specific damage exposures and substitution margins using cross country data. Our decomposition reveals opposing forces: estimated substitution possibilities reduce the welfare cost of a given damage vector, while productivity and temperature uncertainty raise the valuation of climate losses and more than offset this effect. Introducing joint uncertainty about TFP and temperature raises the SCC by 56 percent relative to the deterministic version of our baseline natural-capital model. This increase operates primarily through endogenous changes in expected damages, equilibrium allocation, and discounting, rather than through a conventional covariance risk premium. Carbon pricing therefore requires the joint modeling of physical exposure, production structure, and state-contingent valuation.

title: Environmental Bads
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC) and UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics

detail.title: Environmental Bads
detail.abstract: The existing environmental accounting literature typically uses the Weitzman (1976) consumer perspective to measure the welfare effects of environmental bads (pollution, environmental degradation). We show that the consumer perspective is the “wrong” perspective to measure the welfare effects of bads: it is impossible to measure completely the welfare effects of externalities using a consumer framework based on observed market demand behaviour alone. In contrast, production-based approaches are shown to be useful in this context. We show that when bads are taxed, cost minimization yields a comprehensive cost function that requires no convexity or free disposal assumptions on the technology, and conclude that bads are best netted from the output aggregate rather than treated as inputs.

title: Nature Dependence and Labor Investment Efficiency
affiliations: University of Glasgow, University of Glasgow, University of Zurich - Department Finance and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Nature Dependence and Labor Investment Efficiency
detail.abstract: Does dependence on nature distort how firms hire? Using 86,584 firm-year observations from 68 countries over 2010-2024, we show that it does. More naturedependent firms exhibit lower labor-investment efficiency, driven mainly by underhiring. This inefficiency operates through operational and financial frictions: ESG incidents, market undervaluation, and financing constraints. The effect intensifies where social unrest is frequent, populations are aging, production is skill-intensive, and product-market competition is stronger. It weakens under stricter environmental policy, stronger employment protection, and effective government. Nature dependence is therefore not a purely sustainability concern; it is a binding constraint on firms' employment decisions.

title: Two Accounts of Freedom: Mill vs. Hayek
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Two Accounts of Freedom: Mill vs. Hayek
detail.abstract: John Stuart Mill and Friedrich Hayek were defining theorists of freedom, but they offered very different accounts of both the scope of freedom and its justification. Mill put a bright spotlight on individuals, their knowledge, their potential, and their agency. By contrast, Hayek put a bright spotlight on free markets and traditions, and on government planners and what they do not know and cannot know. Hayek thought that Mill's Harm Principle would protect both too much (because it would operate against the private sphere) and too little (because the notion of harm was too broad). Mill was a romantic about choosers (about individuals, and what they know, and what they are capable of). Hayek endorsed "individualism" above all, but he did not mean, by that term, what Mill meant by "individuality." Hayek was no romantic about individual choosers; he explicitly drew attention to imperfect rationality and human error. Hayek was enthusiastic about undesigned orders and traditions, and a skeptic about planners. Mill was much more skeptical about traditions. These are two faces of liberalism. In important ways, they are complementary, not contradictory. Still, Mill and Hayek had radically different sensibilities.

title: Global Repercussions of EU Climate Policy: Leakage, Retaliation, and Cooperation in an Intertemporal General Equilibrium
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Middle East Technical University (METU) - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global Repercussions of EU Climate Policy: Leakage, Retaliation, and Cooperation in an Intertemporal General Equilibrium
detail.abstract: When a major economy prices carbon unilaterally, the global repercussions of such policy such as carbon leakage, trade retaliation, and the scope for cooperation certainly set the terms of debate over how to advance global mitigation. The European Union (EU), having positioned itself at the forefront of global climate policy, provides a natural case. We examine these repercussions through the EU’s recently launched Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a border measure introduced to combat carbon leakage and align the EU’s climate goals with the patterns of global trade. Covering only a small fraction of the EU imports, the CBAM in isolation is argued to have little impact on the global patterns of trade. Yet, due to its potential threat of triggering retaliatory measures and reformation of distortionary trade clubs, it may have lasting effects inhibiting the potential success of global efforts against climate change.Utilizing a global, multi-regional model that accommodates inter-temporal reallocation effects by forward-looking agents under infinite horizon and inter-temporal optimization, we explore four policy scenarios: first, we invigorate the future pathway of the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) in EU with a projected cap on ETS sectorial emissions extending to 2050. Second, the CBAM is implemented, and its potential macroeconomic and social welfare effects are tabulated. We envisage two opposing responses from the non-EU global economy: (i) instrumentalization of a retaliation tariff rate across the trade partners, to preserve their individual (regional) social welfare against the EU CBAM; and (ii) a scenario of cooperation via full alignment with the EU’s ETS carbon price, accepting the economic rationale of CBAM as a sanctioning instrument. A distinctive feature of our framework is that both the carbon price, determined by an emissions cap, and the strategic responses of trading partners are treated as endogenous equilibrium outcomes rather than imposed exogenously. A global capital market further links investment across regions, so that carbon leakage operates through dynamic capital accumulation and not through static cost-shifting alone. Our analyses show that the reach of unilateral climate policy depends on the strategic responses it elicits covering a broad range from retaliation to cooperation.

title: Inequality, Displacement and the Consequences of Environmental Improvements
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Inequality, Displacement and the Consequences of Environmental Improvements
detail.abstract: Environmental policies aimed at reducing pollution can unintentionally exacerbate environmental injustice through residential sorting. This study examines the effects of environmental improvements on various demographic groups using an instrumental variable approach. Results indicate that lower-income renters and people of color tend to relocate to more polluted neighborhoods and experience shifts in employment and income. Homeowners often remain in improved neighborhoods, benefiting from enhanced environmental quality and property values. Housing tenure and racial identity have profound influence on the distributional impacts of environmental policies, highlighting the importance of enhancing housing affordability and preserving social capital for environmental justice.

title: The Legal AI Supervision Paradox: Cognitive Bias and the Unintended Consequences of Disciplinary Regimes

detail.title: The Legal AI Supervision Paradox: Cognitive Bias and the Unintended Consequences of Disciplinary Regimes
detail.abstract: In this early stage of lawyering with generative artificial intelligence, the legal profession has instituted a categorical double standard.  When human practitioners miss precedents or mischaracterize citations from memory, the conduct is routinely missed or simply tolerated; at worst, it is classified as negligence and absorbed by malpractice regimes. When generative AI produces a functionally identical error, courts and regulators increasingly classify the conduct as reckless, imposing severe sanctions and mandating exhaustive manual verification. Drawing on empirical data from recent benchmarking studies, this Article demonstrates that specialized AI systems in mid-2026 are matching or outperforming human lawyers in aggregate accuracy across multiple legal task domains. The regulatory response requires practitioners to manually re-verify AI outputs using pre-AI methodology, which nullifies the efficiency gains of the technology.  The Article identifies the disparate impact of this verification mandate. The burden falls heavily on solo and small-firm practitioners, who lack the staffing structures required to absorb unbillable verification hours. The Article proposes a harmonized negligence standard, closed-loop safe harbors for certified retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, and evidence-based sanctioning thresholds calibrated to actual human error rates.

title: Green by Demand: Investor Segmentation, Credibility, and Primary Market Demand for Green Bonds
affiliations: University of Strathclyde - Strathclyde Business School, SOAS University of London, University of Strathclyde, Department of Accounting and Finance, University of Strathclyde Business School and

detail.title: Green by Demand: Investor Segmentation, Credibility, and Primary Market Demand for Green Bonds
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of the green bond (GB) market raises questions about how environmental considerations influence investor demand in debt markets. Using detailed orderbook data from  corporate bond issuances, we observe investor demand directly, before market clearing. Consistent with recent evidence, we confirm that GB attract 11.93%-15.03% higher demand multiples than comparable non-GB, equivalent to approximately US$215-US$270 million in additional orders for a median-sized GB issue. Our contribution is to show where and when this premium exists: it is conditional on both regulatory environment and issuer environmental credibility. Higher GB demand is concentrated in markets with stringent sustainable finance regulations, such as the EU, and is absent elsewhere. At the issuer level, environmental credibility, captured by lower carbon intensity, stronger green innovation, and lower ESG-related reputational risk, is associated with significantly stronger GB demand, with the effects being more pronounced in the EU. Results are robust across multiple matching approaches.

title: Between Intrinsic Value and Market Price An Integrated Analysis of Fundamental and Market-Based Equity Valuation: A Case Study of Porsche AG

detail.title: Between Intrinsic Value and Market Price An Integrated Analysis of Fundamental and Market-Based Equity Valuation: A Case Study of Porsche AG
detail.abstract: This paper examines the question of what lies behind a share price from two complementary perspectives: the corporate perspective of fundamental valuation methods and the market perspective of relative valuation and price formation. On the corporate side, the discounted cash flow method (DCF), Economic Value Added (EVA), Economic Profit (EP), the residual income method (Discounted Earning Stream, DES) and the dividend discount model (DDM) are presented systematically and computed in full with real data for a continuous case study-Porsche AG (P911), whose share price has lost roughly 40 per cent since its 2022 initial public offering. On the market side, the paper analyses price formation on the stock exchange, the market model (beta of 1.10 and R² of 0.34 against the DAX), the standard valuation multiples (P/E, P/B, P/S, EV/EBITDA, dividend yield) and the behavioural sources of systematic deviations of price from fundamental value.

title: Corporations and Soft Law: Deliberate Ambiguities
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law

detail.title: Corporations and Soft Law: Deliberate Ambiguities

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Kulick, Lustig, Sanger (eds), OUP Handbook on Corporations and International Law

detail.abstract: This chapter develops a political-economy account of corporate soft law, understood both as soft law made by corporations and as soft law made for corporations by international institutions. It argues that the relationships between hard and soft corporation-related international law, or private and public forms of authority relating to corporations, reproduce, in a different register, the dialectic between property and sovereignty that has accompanied capitalist and colonial expansion since the sixteenth century. Tracing the dialectic evolution of corporate soft law through the medieval and early modern lex mercatoria, the chartered colonial companies, the contractual standards of the industrial and interwar periods, the regulatory standards of contemporary global governance, and the age of platform capitalism and tech companies, the chapter suggests that the ambiguity is a crucial feature of capitalist, imperialist expansion. Soft law and private self-regulation, on this reading, are not marginal or transitional phenomena on the way to binding, publicly sponsored forms of regulation. They are constitutive and recurring instruments of capitalist expansion, alternately shielding corporate power from public regulation and channeling public authority to entrench it. However, disentangling these dialectics becomes difficult in a time where corporations increasingly resemble quasi-sovereign rule-makers in their own right.

title: Reliability-Aware Skin Lesion Decision Support: Cross-DatasetValidation of Selective Prediction, Calibration, and Class-Aware Deferral
affiliations: Alfaisal University, University of Hail and Université de Moncton

detail.title: Reliability-Aware Skin Lesion Decision Support: Cross-DatasetValidation of Selective Prediction, Calibration, and Class-Aware Deferral
detail.abstract: Automated skin-lesion classifiers now approach ceiling performance on benchmark data, yet aggregate accuracy revealslittle about when an individual prediction can be trusted — the property that governs safe clinical use. We reframedermoscopic classification as a reliability-aware selective-prediction problem: rather than only maximizing accuracy,we ask when a model should commit to a prediction and when it should defer to a clinician. The proposed frameworkis evaluated on two publicly available dermoscopic datasets: HAM10000 and the Skin Cancer (ISIC 2018): Malignantvs. Benign dataset. On HAM10000, comprising 10,015 images, we train transparent tree-ensemble classifiers equippedwith a lightweight, retraining-free reliability layer combining maximum class confidence, predictive entropy, post-hoctemperature scaling, and confidence/entropy-based accept–defer rules. Although raw performance on HAM10000 is deliberatelymodest (accuracy 0.709; balanced accuracy 0.395 under severe class imbalance), the reliability layer is highlyinformative: maximum confidence detects incorrect predictions with AUROC 0.811, and temperature scaling reducesexpected calibration error from 0.120 to 0.028 (76.5% reduction). As a decision-support filter, accepting only the mostreliable half of cases raises accepted-case accuracy to 0.905 while routing 83.7% of all errors to expert review. Critically,global confidence deferral is majority-class driven and would still miss many melanomas, whereas a malignancy-awarereferral rule reduces the melanoma miss rate from 26.9% to 7.6% at matched coverage and below 1% at higher deferral.To assess generalizability, the same reliability framework is additionally evaluated on the Skin Cancer (ISIC 2018):Malignant vs. Benign dataset, which comprises 3,297 dermoscopic images, yielding a total of 13,312 images acrossboth cohorts. Reliability behavior remains consistent across datasets: temperature scaling reduces expected calibrationerror from 0.116 to 0.025 on ISIC 2018 (78.2% reduction), confidence-based error detection achieves AUROC 0.817,and selective prediction raises accepted-case accuracy to 0.967 at 50% coverage. These results show that reliabilityassessment, calibration correction, uncertainty-based error detection, and class-aware referral can transform probabilisticclassifiers into more trustworthy decision-support triage systems.

title: Veterinary Health Assessment System (VHAS): AI-Driven Clinical Support for Veterinary Health Assessment and Disease Detection
affiliations: , VIT Bhopal University and VIT Bhopal University

detail.title: Veterinary Health Assessment System (VHAS): AI-Driven Clinical Support for Veterinary Health Assessment and Disease Detection
detail.abstract: The Veterinary Health Assessment System (VHAS), a comprehensive AI-driven multi-model platform that uses more than 85 clinically validated symptoms to perform real-time health risk assessment across 15 animal species, is presented in this paper. To provide precise, understandable, and secure diagnostic support, VHAS combines five machine learning architectures: an MLP neural network, an LSTM sequence model, XGBoost, Random Forest, and an Improved Structured Clinical Transformer (SCT). The system incorporates symptom correlations, severity weights, breed predispositions, and emergency triggers into a large-scale, clinically realistic synthetic dataset of 25,000 veterinary cases. VHAS uses clinical supremacy rule systems, dynamic safety overrides, explainable prediction reporting, and a weighted ensemble inference engine. The ensemble achieves ∼85–87% accuracy and ∼92–93% AUC, while individual model accuracies range from 80–84% and AUC values of 88–92%. These results demonstrate high diagnostic efficacy. For use in telemedicine platforms, emergency triage systems, and veterinary hospitals, VHAS provides a reliable, scalable, and clinically aligned AI architecture.

title: Equivalence-Constrained in-phase/quadrature (IQ) Reconstruction for Penile Ultrasound Vibro-Elastography
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Equivalence-Constrained in-phase/quadrature (IQ) Reconstruction for Penile Ultrasound Vibro-Elastography
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Shear wave elastography (SWE) of the penis is an emerging tool for monitoring erectile dysfunction (ED), but in-phase/quadrature (IQ) signal degradation from poor coupling, motion, and complex anatomy renders many clinical acquisitions unusable. We propose WaveMamba, a lightweight bidirectional reconstruction template restoring complex IQ data prior to local phase-velocity imaging with wave-based filtering (LPVI-WBF), and—equally central—an equivalence-based acceptance criterion determining whether such a front-end is physically faithful. The recommended variant (WaveMamba Conv) uses a bidirectional depth-wise 1-D convolution rather than a selective state-space (SSM) kernel; our ablation shows the SSM kernel confers no advantage, so "WaveMamba" denotes the shared template, not a state-space model.Methods: Five architectures (WaveMamba Conv/Fallback/True, 3D U-Net Lightweight/Full) were trained on Cohort A Good acquisitions and evaluated on three independent test sets: a same-vendor cohort (Cohort B, 6 patients × 4 visits, 700 acquisitions), a multi-vendor out-of-distribution cohort (Cohort A, 66 Borderline), and a synthetic set with reference shear-wave speed (SWS) from the analytical wavefield. Equivalence used TOST; longitudinal effects used linear mixed-effects; demographic correlations used bootstrap 95% CIs.Results: WaveMamba Conv (0.243 M parameters) preserved 97.1% of Cohort B Good and rescued 65.7% of out-of-distribution Borderline scans; it was the only model passing TOST equivalence at all push-frequencies, whereas both 3D U-Net baselines failed at 200 Hz (bias +0.37–0.52 m/s, d = 0.57–0.86). Deployment expanded usable acquisitions from 385 to 517 (+34%), preserved the Erect–Flaccid contrast (Δ = +0.40 m/s at 150 Hz, d = 0.66, p < 0.0001), and revealed a Flaccid SWS decline (β = −0.089 m/s/visit, p = 0.010; visit × state interaction β = −0.096, p = 0.046). Test–retest CVs were 8.1% (Erect) and 11.1% (Flaccid).Conclusions: WaveMamba is a parameter-efficient IQ reconstruction front-end expanding usable SWE acquisitions by 34%; its primary contribution is the equivalence-based acceptance criterion, exposing that pixel-count preservation alone cannot guarantee a faithful quantitative front-end. The reconstructed dataset preserved the Erect–Flaccid contrast and surfaced a candidate longitudinal Flaccid SWS decline; reaching significance only after reconstructed acquisitions are included, it is hypothesis-generating and requires larger multi-center validation

detail.title: A Cross-Attention Survival Network for Early Warning of Acute Clinical Deterioration from Vital-Sign Trajectories
detail.abstract: Background. Acute clinical deterioration in hospitalised patients is a leading cause of preventable in-hospital adverse outcomes. Current early-warning scores depend on static admission-time vital signs and miss the prognostic signal embedded in longitudinal trajectories, while existing machine-learning models require institution-specific feature engineering that limits cross-site applicability.Methods. We conducted a retrospective cohort study at Chonnam National University Hospital (CNUH) comprising 84,049 hourly vital-sign records across 28 features from a Korean general-ward cohort (41 critical events; 4.7 % event rate). We propose TraceSURV (Temporal Representation Attentive Cross-Encoders for Survival Prediction), an end-to-end deep survival network that operates directly on raw multivariate vital-sign sequences without an external feature-engineering pipeline, jointly modeling temporal dynamics and inter-feature interactions via cross-attention. TraceSURV was benchmarked against 18 comparators spanning six methodological families under five-fold cross-validation, and evaluated for architectural generalizability on PhysioNet 2019 Set A (N=20,029) with all models independently retrained on that cohort (not cross-site model transfer).Results. TraceSURV achieved the best tdAUC (0.994 [0.982–0.999]) and best calibration (IBS 0.008 [0.005–0.012]) among all 19 models, and its C-index (0.969 [0.935–0.991]) substantially outperformed clinical early-warning scores (MEWS C = 0.744; NEWS C = 0.741). Given the small primary cohort (41 events), C-index confidence intervals are wide and rankings of the four Tier-1 models overlap (all pairwise p>0.05); TraceSURV's statistically distinguishable advantages were in tdAUC (0.994 vs. 0.980–0.990 for peers) and calibration (IBS 0.008 vs. 0.014–0.022 for peers). In the architectural generalisability experiment, TraceSURV achieved the highest C-index when retrained on PhysioNet (0.916 [0.907–0.923]) with the smallest performance drop (ΔC=−0.053). Attention weights identified Sodium, Platelet, Lactate, and Potassium as the dominant prognostic features, consistent with multi-organ failure pathophysiology; these patterns are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive causal attributions.Conclusion. End-to-end temporal learning on raw vital-sign sequences achieves superior calibration and robust cross-site architectural generalisability, with intrinsic cross-attention weights providing a native clinical interpretation pathway. TraceSURV offers a practical, pipeline-free route to early deterioration detection across heterogeneous clinical environments.

title: A Bioactivity-Grounded Self-Normalizing Neural Network for Drug-Likeness Prediction Beyond Lipinski's Rule of Five
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Furman University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge

detail.title: A Bioactivity-Grounded Self-Normalizing Neural Network for Drug-Likeness Prediction Beyond Lipinski's Rule of Five
detail.abstract: Background and Objectives: Lipinski’s Rule of Five has guided small molecule drug discovery for three decades, but its rigid thresholds exclude biologically active compounds including macrocycles and other complex therapeutics. Existing machine learning models compound this by training on regulatory approval rather than intrinsic bioactivity. This study presentsa bioactivity-grounded neural network for drug-likeness prediction across standard and beyond-Rule-of-Five (bRo5) chemical space.Methods: A four-layer Self-Normalizing Neural Network was trained on 209,259 compounds from ChEMBL 34. Positive labels were assigned to molecules with confirmed binding (half-maximal inhibitory concentration below 50 nM) or clinical advancement through Phases 1 to 4; negatives were compounds with verified inactivity across all recorded assays. Each molecule was encoded as a 1,238-dimensional vector combining 1,024-bit Morgan fingerprints with 214 physicochemical descriptors. Performance was evaluated across five repeated stratified random and scaffold splits. McNemar’s test assessed statistical significance against a LightGBM baseline and a Chemprop graph neural network.Results: On a 15% holdout (n = 31,391), the model achieved 93.45% accuracy and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.9777, outperforming both baselines (p = 2.30 × 10-45; p = 0.0126). Sensitivity on held-out clinical candidates was 94.43%. Precision and specificity for the piecewise surrogate were 75.47% and 75.46% (standard molecules) and76.24% and 76.22% (beyond-Rule-of-Five compounds), respectively. Scaffold generalization reached 87.63% accuracy.Conclusions: The model’s decision boundary was distilled into a piecewise scoring formula stratified by molecular weight. For standard molecules (MW < 500 Da): Z = - 7.1577 + 2.6147 (BCUT2D_CHGHI) + 0.0544 (fr_Ar_N) + 0.0208 (TPSA) + 0.1122 (EState_VSA2) + 0.0602 (EState_VSA10) + 0.3898 (RingCount)+ 0.3284 (Chi1n) + 0.0026 (BertzCT) + 0.3701 (NumHAcceptors)- 1.8925 (FractionCSP3)For bRo5 molecules (MW ≥ 500 Da):Z = - 17.2985 + 8.1213 (BCUT2D_CHGHI) + 0.1382 (fr_Ar_N) + 0.0104 (TPSA)+ 0.0406 (EState_VSA2) - 0.0368 (EState_VSA10) + 0.4550 (NumArHetero)- 0.9592 (fr_guanido) - 0.2622 (RingCount) - 0.0095 (SMR_VSA6)- 0.1402 (Chi1n)with P = 1/(1+e-Z) in both cases. This enables rapid manual triage withoutspecialized software.

title: A Lightweight CNN-BiLSTM Framework for Sleep Stage Classification from Raw Single-Channel EEG
affiliations: Babol Noshirvani University of Technology, Babol Noshirvani University of Technology and Babol Noshirvani University of Technology

detail.title: A Lightweight CNN-BiLSTM Framework for Sleep Stage Classification from Raw Single-Channel EEG
detail.abstract: Sleep plays a crucial role in physical and mental health, and sleep staging is a key step in evaluating sleep quality and diagnosing sleep-related disorders. Manual scoring is time-consuming and can vary across scorers, which has motivated automated methods based on machine learning and deep learning. This study presents an end-to-end sleep stage classification approach that operates directly on raw single-channel EEG recorded from the Fpz–Cz derivation. The recordings are segmented into standard 30-second epochs, and short sequences of consecutive epochs are used to incorporate local temporal context. The model combines a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional feature extractor with bidirectional sequence modeling to capture stage transitions, producing predictions in the five-class setting W, N1, N2, N3, and R. Experiments on multiple releases from the Sleep-EDF Expanded family show strong overall performance, achieving 92.9% accuracy and 83.1% macro F1-score, while improving sensitivity to the challenging N1 stage with an F1-score of 59%. These results indicate that the proposed method can provide an effective and computationally efficient solution for automated sleep stage classification.

title: Latent Space Whitening for Robust Medical Image Segmentation:Block-Based Cholesky Orthogonalization and ArchitecturalVulnerabilities
affiliations: Alfaisal University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Université de Moncton, University of Hail and Université de Moncton

detail.title: Latent Space Whitening for Robust Medical Image Segmentation:Block-Based Cholesky Orthogonalization and ArchitecturalVulnerabilities
detail.abstract: While volumetric deep convolutional neural networks achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on in-distribution clinical images,they remain highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution domain shifts such as sensor noise and spatial smoothing.To cultivate robust latent features, this manuscript introduces a novel block-based, cross-channel Cholesky decorrelationmodule (Latent Whitening) that enforces an orthogonal latent projection directly within the network bottleneck.We subject this proposed architectural constraint, alongside latent volumetric regularization (LVolReg) that penalizes themini-batch variance of the latent log-determinant, to a rigorous, mechanics-focused evaluation under systematic clinicalcorruption fields, uncovering unexpected regional trade-offs, severe architectural dependencies, and numerical vulnerabilities.Evaluating these strategies across a multi-seed bootstrap framework demonstrates that our orthogonal Choleskyprojection module acts as a broad-spectrum shield against additive noise, securing consistent and statistically robustgains over both standard baselines (up to d = +0.78) and channel-wise normalization (up to d = +0.65). Conversely, ourstress testing exposes a critical structural vulnerability under heavy spatial blur strictly bounded to traditional 3D U-Nettopologies, where whitening triggers an escalation in mask failures due to matrix ill-conditioning—a degradation notobserved in residual (ResUNet) shortcut architectures. Finally, we reveal that constraining latent-volume homogeneityacts as a uniform detriment to inference stability rather than a benign spatial trade-off. Ultimately, our findings validatethe efficiency of the proposed orthogonal projection while charting its precise structural boundaries, offering a clearblueprint for engineering robust volumetric medical vision backbones.

title: Glucoformer: Multimodal Cross-subject Glucose Forecasting with Long-term Prediction Capability
affiliations: Central South University, Central South University, Central South University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Central South University and Central South University

detail.title: Glucoformer: Multimodal Cross-subject Glucose Forecasting with Long-term Prediction Capability
detail.abstract: Background and ObjectiveType 1 diabetes (T1D) leads to various severe complications, and precise blood glucose (BG) forecasting is essential for disease management. Glucose metabolism shows complex nonlinear characteristics and large individual differences, while carbohydrate, insulin and other factors jointly affect glycemic fluctuations. Existing models have limited cross-subject generalization and weak long-term prediction performance. This study develops Glucoformer for multimodal multi-horizon glucose forecasting.MethodsGlucoformer optimizes the Crossformer architecture through three targeted modules, including Statistical-Aware Segment Embedding, Enhanced Two-Stage Attention and a simplified Refined Decoder. A pretrain-finetune transfer learning pipeline is applied: the model is pre-trained on simulated T1DMS dataset, fine-tuned and internally validated on OhioT1DM with its held-out test subset, and further evaluated via zero-shot inference on independent DiaTrend dataset. Prediction horizons of 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes are adopted. We compare the proposed model with mainstream time series forecasting models using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Parkes Error Grid Analysis.ResultsOn OhioT1DM, Glucoformer lowers RMSE by 13.06%~34.98% and MAE by 18.65%~42.06% against baseline models, and reduces RMSE by 1.27%~5.48% and MAE by 1.47%~7.99% compared with SOTA methods. Its RMSE values at 30/60/90/120 min are 16.88, 28.10, 36.31, 41.90 mg/dL, with corresponding MAE of 12.07, 20.74, 27.40, 32.20 mg/dL, and around 97.5% of its predictions fall within clinically safe A+B zones at the 120-min horizon. On external DiaTrend dataset, Glucoformer reduces RMSE by 1.01%~19.31% and MAE by 0.30%~24.26% over competing models, with RMSE of 23.06, 36.93, 45.87, 51.61 mg/dL and MAE of 16.55, 27.56, 35.13, 40.25 mg/dL, and approximately 96.0% of predictions staying in clinically safe A+B zones at the 120-min horizon. Ablation, attention and computational complexity analyses verify the effectiveness of model designs.ConclusionsGlucoformer gains moderate performance improvement at different horizons and shows acceptable cross-subject generalization, which can support multimodal long-term glucose prediction in practical scenarios.

title: A real world application of artificial intelligence (AI)-based breast cancer recurrence risk prediction model

detail.title: A real world application of artificial intelligence (AI)-based breast cancer recurrence risk prediction model
detail.abstract: Objective: Accurate prediction of breast cancer (BC) recurrence after curative treatment is essential for optimizing surveillance strategies and personalized patient management. We aimed to prospectively validate a previously developed artificial intelligence (AI)-based breast cancer recurrence prediction model in a real-world clinical setting.Methods: This prospective real-world validation study included BC patients who underwent curative surgery followed by adjuvant therapy at a tertiary cancer center. The AI model integrated clinicopathologic variables and longitudinal follow-up data, including laboratory and imaging findings, to estimate individualized 2-year recurrence risk. Patients were stratified into low- and high-risk groups based on a predefined risk threshold. Model performance was evaluated using recurrence outcomes during follow-up.Results: Of 829 patients initially identified, 400 were included in the final analysis after applying the eligibility criteria. The model classified 391 patients (97.8%) as low risk and 9 (2.2%) as high risk. During the predefined two-year follow-up period, 7 patients (1.8%) developed recurrence, including 6 in the low-risk group (1.5%) and 1 in the high-risk group (11.1%). The model demonstrated excellent specificity (98.0%) and negative predictive value (98.5%) for identifying patients at low risk of recurrence.Conclusion: Prospective real-world validation demonstrated that the AI-based prediction model effectively identified patients at low risk of breast cancer recurrence. These findings support the clinical feasibility of AI-assisted recurrence risk stratification for personalized post-treatment surveillance, although further external validation in larger multi-center cohorts is warranted.

title: Divergence-Constrained Deep Learning for Super-Resolution Reconstruction of Transient Aneurysmal Flow Fields
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Divergence-Constrained Deep Learning for Super-Resolution Reconstruction of Transient Aneurysmal Flow Fields
detail.abstract: Background and Objective:Reconstructing high-fidelity cardiovascular flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements remains a major challenge in computational hemodynamics, particularly for patient-specific aneurysm simulations where imaging modalities provide limited spatial resolution and measurement uncertainty. This study aims to develop a physics-constrained deep learning framework for super-resolution reconstruction of transient aneurysmal flow fields from degraded velocity data.Methods:A high-fidelity dataset is generated by solving the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations using a finite element formulation in an idealized aneurysm geometry under pulsatile inflow conditions. The resulting velocity fields are degraded using spatial downsampling and additive Gaussian noise to emulate limitations of four-dimensional flow magnetic resonance imaging. A U-Net-based convolutional neural network is trained to reconstruct high-resolution velocity fields. Physical consistency is enforced through a divergence-based regularization term derived from the incompressibility constraint.Results:The proposed divergence-constrained model achieves improved reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing divergence magnitude compared to unconstrained training. A parametric study over different penalty weights demonstrates a consistent trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and mass conservation, with optimal settings achieving substantial improvements in physical consistency without degrading flow structure prediction.Conclusions:The proposed framework provides an efficient computational strategy for integrating high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulations with physics-constrained deep learning for cardiovascular flow reconstruction under realistic imaging degradation conditions.

title: Deep Neural Network-Based Current Optimization for Polyrhythmic Multifocal Brain Stimulation
affiliations: Korea Brain Research Institute and Korea Brain Research Institute

detail.title: Deep Neural Network-Based Current Optimization for Polyrhythmic Multifocal Brain Stimulation
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Multifocal transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) has emerged as a promising approach for modulating distributed brain networks. However, conventional multifocal tACS typically applies a single common stimulation frequency across multiple electrodes. Delivering distinct frequencies to multiple target regions remains technically challenging because simultaneously injected currents can induce spatial crosstalk and unintended frequency interference. To address this issue, we propose a deep neural network (DNN)-based optimization framework for polyrhythmic multifocal brain stimulation that independently determines the current amplitude and frequency assignment of each electrode to achieve frequency-specific targeting.Methods: We developed a DNN architecture that simultaneously optimizes the stimulation frequency and current amplitude of each electrode using a single constant input without requiring external training data. The framework incorporates safety constraints and a minimum physiological electric-field threshold into the optimization process. Using realistic head models obtained from 20 subjects, we compared the performance of the proposed DNN framework with that of conventional genetic algorithm (GA)-based optimization methods.Results: The DNN framework successfully achieved spatial separation of frequency-specific electric fields, enabling each stimulation frequency to be selectively concentrated within its intended target region while minimizing unintended frequency interference in non-target regions. Moreover, the DNN framework demonstrated significantly superior performance to that of GA-based methods in terms of concentration ratio and frequency-specific selectivity. Computational efficiency was also substantially improved, reducing the average optimization time from more than 30 minutes to approximately 1.6 minutes.Conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient, safety-constrained polyrhythmic multifocal stimulation through the spatial separation of distinct frequency-specific electric fields. This approach may facilitate individualized network-level neuromodulation for cognitive enhancement and the treatment of neuropsychiatric disorders.

title: When Accuracy Saturates, Reliability Leads: A Staged Evaluation ofUncertainty Estimators for 3D Pancreas Segmentation
affiliations: Alfaisal University, Université de Moncton, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Hail and Université de Moncton

detail.title: When Accuracy Saturates, Reliability Leads: A Staged Evaluation ofUncertainty Estimators for 3D Pancreas Segmentation
detail.abstract: Architectural innovation on three-dimensional medical image segmentation increasingly yields diminishing returns: onwell-posed tasks a competent backbone already recovers most of the available spatial signal, so accuracy saturatesand additional modules move it little. We argue that in this regime the actionable axis is reliability rather than accuracy,and we test this claim through a staged protocol grounded in the Unified Variational Intelligence Framework(UVIF), whose uncertainty term becomes the natural target once the task loss plateaus. On the Medical SegmentationDecathlon pancreas task (281 CT volumes; pancreas and mass classes), Stage 1 establishes saturation: under a controlledmulti-seed protocol with a fixed held-out test set and Holm-corrected paired tests, neither a learnable Fourierband-pass module, a learnable Fresnel-propagation module, nor an edge-attention reference improves Dice over a plainresidual U-Net. Stage 2 reuses the trained models, without retraining, to evaluate five uncertainty estimators as failuredetectors. Deep-ensemble disagreement is significantly better calibrated and more reliable than single-model confidence(failure-detection AUROC 0.80 vs. 0.74; expected calibration error 0.075 vs. 0.156; all p < 10 −4 ). In contrast,two physics-motivated single-pass estimators derived from Fresnel diffraction—feature-space coherence and decisionspaceview-disagreement—underperform even trivial softmax entropy. We conclude that ensembling, not architecturalor single-pass physics priors, delivers reliable uncertainty on accuracy-saturated segmentation, and that ensemble disagreementfurnishes a concrete estimator for the UVIF uncertainty term.

title: A Digital Twin Framework for Hourly Carbon Accounting: Adaptive Mobile Monitoring Routing and Optimal Stopping
affiliations: Jiangsu University and Jiangsu University

detail.title: A Digital Twin Framework for Hourly Carbon Accounting: Adaptive Mobile Monitoring Routing and Optimal Stopping
detail.abstract: Carbon accounting of an industrial point source still cannot deliver unannounced, hourly verification: the emission-factor method is retrospective and biased, in-fence monitoring needs firm cooperation, and off-site unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flights use fixed routes that are wind-fragile and waste energy. We introduce a digital-twin adaptive unmanned aerial vehicle inspection that, after each hover sample, plans the next waypoint by information gain per flight energy and stops once a prescribed tolerance is met, turning one battery cycle into a reproducible, off-site, hourly measurement. Efficient onboard replanning keeps planning millisecond-fast and guarantees the campaign closes in a single sortie. Across twelve cement-clinker campaigns the method reproduces the true hourly emission rate with 3.0 per cent mean absolute error and 8.0 per cent relative standard deviation while using 9.5 waypoints and 250 Wh, 46 to 64 per cent less energy than fixed routes at equal or better accuracy. The default emission-factor benchmark overestimates the mean by 6.1 per cent and misses the intra-day profile by up to 14.5 per cent. The approach gives regulators and operators a low-cost, unannounced monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) capability that corrects factor-method bias, properly rewards genuine emission reductions, and strengthens the credibility of carbon markets, border-adjustment mechanisms and corporate net-zero claims.

title: A Reproducible Framework for Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction in Medical Image Classification
affiliations: Federal University of São Carlos

detail.title: A Reproducible Framework for Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction in Medical Image Classification
detail.abstract: Background and Objective. Marginal conformal prediction guarantees can hold even when clinically important diagnostic classes remain under-covered, especially under the class imbalance common in biomedical image classification. This study presents a reproducible evaluation pipeline for auditing conformal prediction beyond marginal validity.Methods. Given stored probability arrays, labels, split indices, class mappings, and provenance manifests, the pipeline compares standard conformal prediction, adaptive and regularized adaptive prediction sets, Mondrian/classwise calibration, and frequency-grouped calibration. It reports marginal, per-class, prevalence-stratified, and size-stratified coverage with bootstrap confidence intervals and per-class below-target tests, and includes non-destructive split, overlap, and duplicate-checking utilities.Results. On an eight-class ISIC 2019 dermatoscopic classification task using a fixed ResNet-50 checkpoint, standard conformal prediction reached 0.8995 marginal coverage at 90% target coverage yet nominally under-covered five of eight classes. Per-class coverage ranged from 0.6667 for actinic keratosis to 0.9662 for melanocytic nevus, and the descriptive high-versus-low prevalence coverage gap was 0.1900. Mondrian/classwise calibration reduced this gap to 0.0189 while increasing average set size from 2.04 to 2.67. Frequency-grouped calibration reduced it to 0.0408 at average set size 2.50.Conclusions. Biomedical conformal prediction studies should report class-conditional reliability, dataset provenance, and overlap structure alongside marginal validity.

title: Framework: A Process Architecture for Sequential Strategic Decision-Making
affiliations: and

detail.title: Framework: A Process Architecture for Sequential Strategic Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Purpose-The G.A.C.E.™ Framework (Han and Walsh, 2025c) proposed four sequential components for strategic decision-making under uncertainty: Global Analysis, Actionable Insights, Conclusion, and Execution. This paper does not restate that architecture; it theorises how the framework operates as a process, specifying the internal logic of each stage and the mechanisms connecting them. Design/methodology/approach-This is a conceptual paper. It develops an input-process-output architecture for each G.A.C.E.™ stage, integrating literature on dynamic-capability microfoundations, organisational sensemaking, multi-criteria decision making and strategy implementation, and advances six theoretically derived propositions. Findings-The framework's explanatory value resides less in its four components individually than in the transition logic connecting them and the closure of the feedback loop from Execution back to Global Analysis. The A.C.T.I.O.N.™ Decision Matrix (Han and Walsh, 2025a) is situated within Conclusion as one operationalisation of multi-criteria evaluation, not a self-contained novelty. Originality-The paper's principal contribution is a process-level theorisation of the transitions connecting G.A.C.E.™'s four stages: how information becomes insight, insight becomes bounded choice, choice becomes executable action, and execution outcomes re-enter analysis. The validity of this theorisation is supported by an input-process-output specification, a six-criterion actionability filter and six conceptual propositions. A subsequent paper is positioned as a synthetic scenario-based stress test of these propositions and their boundary conditions, rather than as empirical validation; independent field validation remains a later research requirement.

title: Stress-Testing G.A.C.E. 1 : A Synthetic Scenario Study of Robustness and Boundary Conditions
affiliations: and

detail.title: Stress-Testing G.A.C.E. 1 : A Synthetic Scenario Study of Robustness and Boundary Conditions
detail.abstract: Purpose-This paper examines whether an integrative strategic decision framework behaves as theorised once its mechanisms are stress-tested under deliberately varied and adverse synthetic conditions, and what this reveals about the framework's boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach-Four synthetic decision scenarios, plus a minimal boundary case, are constructed to vary systematically in uncertainty, analysis protocol, alternative separation, veto exposure and compliance salience all author-constructed and disclosed as such. Each scenario applies an identical four-stage decision protocol and a five-criterion evaluation matrix. Robustness is examined through full one-at-a-time weight perturbation across all five criteria and a complete bounded score-stress test, rather than a single-criterion check. Two scenario conditions hold the same underlying factual information constant while varying only how it is processed, to distinguish the consequences of structured encoding from differences in information content within the constructed comparison. and further testing, including a tentative view on when a full four-stage evaluation process is and is not likely to be worth its overhead. Originality-The paper's principal contribution is a transparent, adversarial synthetic stress-testing protocol for examining an integrative strategic decision framework's internal mechanisms and boundary conditions, without overstating synthetic evidence as empirical validation. This protocol rests on three supporting methodological components: a construct distinction, introduced for this study, between an insight's admissibility and its power to discriminate between alternatives; a robustness analysis that separates weight instability from score instability rather than treating perturbation as a single undifferentiated test; and an explicit evidence-strength hierarchy that keeps mechanism demonstration, scenario-conditional evidence and empirical validation from being described in the same terms.

title: Beyond Socioeconomic Status: System-Level Determinants of Drinking Water Violations Across U.S. Counties

detail.title: Beyond Socioeconomic Status: System-Level Determinants of Drinking Water Violations Across U.S. Counties

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Access to safe drinking water remains an unresolved public health challenge in the United States. While prior research has linked drinking water violations to socioeconomic disadvantage and racial composition, most studies rely on limited geographic scope or struggle with mapping water systems to counties in federal databases. This study overcomes a longstanding data limitation in the EPA's Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) by developing a validated county namematching approach that achieves 99.9% mapping accuracy across all 50 states. Using this method, I analyze 41,955 unique health-based drinking water violations from 47,679 community water systems across 3,070 U.S. counties for the 2019-2023 period. Sequential regression models reveal that commonly cited socioeconomic indicators alone explain very little variation in county-level violation rates (R² = 0.011). Adding racial/ethnic composition and rural-urban classification modestly improves explanatory power (R² = 0.029). However, system-level infrastructure characteristics (including the number of water systems per county, average system size, and water source type) nearly triple the explained variance (R² = 0.089). Poverty rate, Hispanic population share, and rural status are consistently significant predictors, but the strongest driver of violations is the structural fragmentation of local water systems. These findings suggest that efforts to improve drinking water safety should prioritize system-level capacity building alongside socioeconomic targeting.

title: Eco-Onenessism: An Environmental Ethics of Interconnectedness for Addressing Climate Change
affiliations: University of Delta Agbor Delta state

detail.title: Eco-Onenessism: An Environmental Ethics of Interconnectedness for Addressing Climate Change
detail.abstract: Climate change represents one of the most pressing global challenges of the 21st century. The rising of global temperatures, extreme weather events, melting ice caps, and shifting ecosystems are impacts of climate change. The moral implications of climate change have far-reaching effects on biodiversity, global stability, and ecological well-being. Using the philosophical method of analysis, the study finds that the cause of climate change is the human inability to see Earth as one and the lack of oneness; the ecological trinity in the hierarchy of being. The objective of the study is to recommend eco-onenessism by policymakers through teaching and learning in schools to affirm the unity of existence in the state of being. This philosophy stresses the interconnectedness of nature. Although the study finds that the implementation of Eco-onenessism is challenged by human anthropocentrism, yet it offers humanity a comprehensive framework that aligns environmental preservation with a sustainable future.

title: Social Synchronization Blueprint Synchronizing Wealth, Governance, and Human Capability

detail.title: Social Synchronization Blueprint Synchronizing Wealth, Governance, and Human Capability

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) represent one of the most significant institutional innovations in modern public finance, preserving collective wealth across generations while promoting fiscal stability and long-term investment. Traditionally, these institutions have been evaluated according to financial performance, asset diversification, and macroeconomic resilience. While these measures remain essential, they capture only one dimension of institutional success.

This monograph proposes a broader analytical framework that evaluates sovereign wealth funds according to their capacity to transform collective wealth into collective human capability. Through a comparative analysis of four internationally recognized models—Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, Australia's Future Fund, the Alaska Permanent Fund, and Singapore's Temasek Holdings—the study examines the relationships among economic prosperity, institutional governance, and citizen well-being.

Using comparative economic indicators, internationally recognized governance metrics, and findings from the World Happiness Report, the analysis explores whether financial success alone adequately explains differences in human flourishing or whether institutional quality functions as the principal mechanism through which wealth becomes societal well-being. The comparative evidence suggests that sovereign wealth funds successfully preserve financial capital across diverse political and economic systems. However, economic prosperity alone does not consistently predict higher levels of reported well-being. Rather, governance quality, institutional trust, public services, and long-term policy coherence appear to influence how collective wealth is translated into human opportunity.

Building upon these findings, this monograph introduces the Social Synchronization Blueprint (SSB), an institutional design model proposing that long-term societal progress emerges when independent systems—including governance, markets, science, technology, healthcare, education, and civil society—become intentionally synchronized toward the expansion of collective human capability. Within this framework, sovereign wealth funds are examined not as isolated financial institutions, but as one component of a broader institutional architecture through which intelligence, public wealth, and technological progress become enduring human flourishing.

Rather than advocating a particular political ideology, this work contributes to the fields of institutional design, public administration, systems science, and governance by proposing a multidisciplinary framework for evaluating how intelligent societies organize collective resources across generations.

title: Psychological Counseling in the World of Work

detail.title: Psychological Counseling in the World of Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is President of the Verband Psychologischer Berater e.V. (VpsyB), Lead Lecturer at the Akademie Psychologischer Berater, and Honorary Professor of Counseling Psychology. She therefore represents institutional interests in the field of non-medical psychological counseling; the initiative mentioned in this paper is co-sponsored by VpsyB e.V. The paper is intended as a scientific assessment of the field; the roles stated above are disclosed in the interest of transparency. No third party funding was received for its preparation. To the author's knowledge, there are no other financial or personal conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve any studies with human participants or animals. It is based exclusively on the analysis of publicly available data, legal sources, and scientific literature. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external or third-party funding was received for this research. The work was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The world of work is one of the central settings in which mental strain arises, becomes visible, and generates economic costs in Germany. Absence days attributable to mental disorders continue to reach new record levels, and mental disorders are among the most common causes of early retirement. The demands of Work 4.0 and New Work—digitalization, the blurring of boundaries, acceleration, and increasing complexity—further intensify this strain.

This paper argues that this development can be addressed neither by treatment within the scope of the legally defined practice of medicine and healing (Heilkunde) nor by structural occupational safety measures alone. Rather, individual primary prevention is required that intervenes before strain develops into disorders requiring treatment. Non-medical psychological counseling is described as a low-threshold, resource-oriented, confidential service that is clearly delineated from the practice of medicine and healing and can close this gap.

This paper was originally written in German by the author. AI-assisted translation tool (Open AI) was used solely for a literal, word-for-word translation into English, without any content changes. The author reviewed and verified the translated text for accuracy.

title: Organizing the Cup: NASCAR, Antitrust, and the Business of Cup Series Charters
affiliations: University of Arizona

detail.title: Organizing the Cup: NASCAR, Antitrust, and the Business of Cup Series Charters
detail.abstract: Sports championships demand coordination, but centralized control can also give an organizer power over the teams whose investment and competition make the championship possible. This case study explores that tension through the antitrust lawsuit brought by 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports challenging NASCAR’s Cup Series charter system. Although the charters guaranteed race entry and revenue distributions, they afforded teams neither equity nor governance rights. The plaintiffs alleged that NASCAR foreclosed access to the complementary inputs needed to establish a rival premier stock-car racing series, thereby preserving its monopsony power. NASCAR countered that the challenged arrangements safeguarded investment incentives, safety, product quality, and goodwill. This case study places the parties’ claims within the economics of championship production while distinguishing among unilateral conduct, vertical agreements, and horizontal coordination among teams. The parties settled during trial and announced a form of evergreen charter, leaving unresolved questions of liability, antitrust injury, damages, and competitive effects. This case study illustrates how value creation and market power can coexist—and why sports-antitrust analysis must carefully assess challenged restraints, their effects and justifications, and the availability of less restrictive alternatives.

title: The Shape of the Shadow: Learnable Theory and the Puzzle of What We Fail to See

detail.title: The Shape of the Shadow: Learnable Theory and the Puzzle of What We Fail to See

detail.abstract: When we fail to notice something in plain view, is that failure a kind of judgement that the thing isn't there, or simply a case of not expecting it? Miller (2026) argues that such omissions are not blank gaps but structured mental states with real epistemic consequences, and asks which of these two readings, a modal one or a probabilistic one, correctly describes their content. She leaves the question open. This paper argues that the question rests on a false choice between two options where there are really three. The extra option follows from Learnable Theory's central claim: that shared representations of reality occupy their own layer, the Learnable, an intersubjective plane built and maintained largely through language, and shaped by the specific structures a language provides for organising meaning, its lexicon, grammar, syntax, semantics, and pragmatics (Magni, Marchetti, & Alharbi, 2023). Three of the devices that organise this layer, relators, nouns, and adjectives, back information away from attention in three structurally different ways, only one of them genuinely modal, only one genuinely probabilistic, with the third belonging to neither category. I show how this distinction resolves Miller's central case, generates a prediction that could actually be tested, and extends naturally to explain a familiar and consequential kind of organisational blindness.

title: The Multinational Wage Premium: Production vs. Financial Networks
affiliations: University of Bayreuth - Department of Economics and Institute for Employment Research (IAB)

detail.title: The Multinational Wage Premium: Production vs. Financial Networks
detail.abstract: This paper studies the relationship between multinational ownership and wages paid by German manufacturing plants. We provide novel evidence that the sizable multinational wage premium in our data is significantly smaller when plants are owned by financial investors. This observed wage gap is particularly pronounced in environments with collective bargaining and cross-border production structures. Evidence on patent citations further suggests that technology linkages within ownership networks are associated with higher wages in general, but less so when plants are owned by financial investors. To interpret these patterns, we develop a general equilibrium model of trade with oligopolistic product market competition and collective wage bargaining. In the model, multinational ownership can shape wages through two channels: it strengthens firms' outside options in wage negotiations, facilitating surplus appropriation in financial networks, and it can create additional surplus through the exploitation of cross-border production synergies in production networks. The latter channel is relevant only if the owner is not a financial investor, highlighting the central role of ownership structure for the labor market effects of multinational activity.

detail.abstract:
The digital wellbeing industry — spanning tele-counselling, guided yoga and breathwork, trauma-informed therapy adjuncts, and AI-driven life coaching — has largely inherited its success metrics from consumer and social media applications: daily active users, streaks, session counts, and retention curves.

These are engagement metrics, optimised for attention capture, and they are poorly suited to platforms whose stated purpose is durable behavior change rather than sustained app dependency. For a therapeutic or wellness context, high engagement and genuine transformation can diverge sharply: a user who logs in daily for years without measurable change in wellbeing outcomes registers as a retention success and a clinical failure.

This paper introduces the Value Realisation Index (VRI), a composite measurement framework built on four sub-domains — Practice Depth, Outcome Delta, Autonomy Transfer, and Reward-to-Value Ratio — designed to distinguish platforms that facilitate genuine behavior transformation from those that merely optimise for stickiness.

Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and situated against the emerging "engagement–efficacy–ethics" literature on gamified digital mental health, the VRI reframes the ideal user trajectory as one of rising autonomy and falling platform dependency, rather than indefinite engagement growth.

We construct the index, illustrate its application across counselling, yoga/breathwork, and life-coaching modalities, and discuss its implications for product design, investor diligence, and emerging digital-wellbeing governance in India and other Global South markets building AI-native health infrastructure.

We close with a proposed research agenda for empirical validation.

title: Financial Inclusion and Electricity Uptake
affiliations: World Bank’s Development Research Group and

detail.title: Financial Inclusion and Electricity Uptake
detail.abstract: Even as governments push to build infrastructure to achieve universal access to electricity, demand-side barriers constrain uptake where infrastructure already exists. This paper assesses the impact of the quasi-experimental introduction of mobile money on electricity adoption by households. We conduct a granular district-level analysis of 33 sub-Saharan African countries that leverages differential sub-national mobile network coverage. We find that mobile money access improves district-level power uptake by around 24% relative to similar districts without mobile money access. We provide evidence consistent with demand-side channels, specifically reduced financial frictions, driving this relationship as opposed to supply-side infrastructure expansion. Furthermore, we highlight the enabling role of mobile network coverage and the detrimental impact of mobile money taxes on electrification efforts.
