detail.abstract: What should we, as Californians and Americans, do to ensure that no child is left unattended in a car? Our hearts break a little for every story in the paper about a child who has been left in a hot car by a hurried and distracted parent. For many of us who know the difficulties of modern parenting, when juggling childcare and careers, we are forced to identify with the caregivers who are perhaps sleep deprived from nightly feedings or distracted by an abrupt change in routine, and we wish that there were more resources available to these parents and their children. But instead of looking for ways to solve the problems of distractedness and help caregivers with better support, all too often society seems to blame and prosecute caregivers after tragic accidents.

title: Inflation Targeting and Zero Lower Bound Risk: Cross-Country Evidence
affiliations: ISEG Lisbon School of Economics and Management,Universidade de Lisboa and ISEG Lisbon School of Economics and Management,Universidade de Lisboa

detail.title: Inflation Targeting and Zero Lower Bound Risk: Cross-Country Evidence
detail.abstract: In the aftermath of the 2007-2009 global financial crisis, a growing body of research questioned the conventional inflation-targeting framework that has long guided monetary policy, arguing that the inflation targets adopted by major central banks may have been set too low. We evaluate the likelihood that advanced economies will become constrained by the effective lower bound on nominal interest rates in the future. Therefore, using end-quarter data over the period 1999Q1 to 2025Q4, we develop a counterfactual framework that quantifies how this risk changes under alternative scenarios with higher average inflation. Using a vector autoregression model and an ARDL-ECM framework, we estimate the cumulative probability of hitting the Zero Lower Bound (ZLB), that is, the probability that policy rates reach the constraint at least once during the projection horizon. Our results indicate that Switzerland and Japan face the highest risk of encountering the ZLB, whereas Sweden, the Euro Area, the United States, and Canada exhibit an intermediate level of risk. By contrast, the United Kingdom and Norway appear to be the least vulnerable. These findings are broadly consistent with cross-country differences in average inflation and nominal interest rate levels.

title: The Law of Restitution for Void Contracts: An Economic Analysis
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law and George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: The Law of Restitution for Void Contracts: An Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops an economic analysis of the application of the law of restitution to the case of void contracts, when agreements may be unenforceable due to legal invalidity. It develops a simple model in which contracting parties’ agreements potentially impose external harms. The analysis focuses on how alternative restitution regimes affect contracting incentives when there is a possibility that agreements may turn out to be unenforceable. A central insight is that in a setting in which contract invalidity is possible, contracting requires not merely that the parties’ joint surplus is positive but also that a participation constraint is satisfied for each party (as there are states of the world in which the parties cannot redistribute the surplus between themselves). We show that full restitution can induce socially excessive contracting, while the denial of restitution can inefficiently deter welfare-enhancing transactions. A regime of partial restitution can potentially implement first-best outcomes by calibrating parties’ incentives to the probability and magnitude of potential external harms. In essence, this regime can serve as a substitute for a Pigovian tax on the contracting parties. The paper discusses applications of this framework to the interest rate swap cases of the 1990s and to other contexts.

title: The Limits of a Broad VAT Cut: Pass-Through Heterogeneity and Welfare Interpretation
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department and University of Cologne

detail.title: The Limits of a Broad VAT Cut: Pass-Through Heterogeneity and Welfare Interpretation
detail.abstract: This paper studies heterogeneity in the pass-through of Germany's temporary VAT reduction in July 2020. Using confidential product-level CPI data, we document substantial dispersion in consumer-price responses: nearly half of standard-rate products show no consumer-price change, while 30 percent exhibit full pass-through. Lower-income households experienced somewhat larger proportional price declines than higher-income households. Using an inverse-optimality consistency test, we show that, once the full revenue loss is considered, the reform cannot be rationalized by any progressive weighting of gains across income groups.

title: The Limits of Coercive Pronatalist Policy: Evidence from Romania's Decree 770
affiliations: Cato Institute - Center for Global Liberty and Prosperity and

detail.title: The Limits of Coercive Pronatalist Policy: Evidence from Romania's Decree 770
detail.abstract: Romania's Decree 770 banned abortion and restricted contraception from 1966 to 1989. We use the synthetic control method to estimate its effect on birth rates, constructing a counterfactual Romania from a donor pool of communist countries. Romanian birth rates rose approximately 90 percent in 1967, and the total fertility rate (TFR) nearly doubled from 1.9 to 3.66. Romania's treatment effect ranked first in the placebo distribution from 1967 through 1969. The effect attenuated as Romanians adapted but re-emerged after enforcement tightened in 1985. Our counterfactual estimates indicate that Decree 770 added approximately 1.7 million people to Romania's population by 1989, closing roughly half the gap between the no-intervention population trajectory and the government's target. Fertility collapsed after repeal in December 1989 and became indistinguishable from neighboring countries. Romania's experience represents an outer bound of natalist policy effectiveness and suggests that moderate policy is unlikely to reverse fertility decline, even if it may dampen it.

title: Corporate Democratic Responsibility: The Role of Companies in Supporting Democracy
affiliations: Dresden University of Technology and

detail.title: Corporate Democratic Responsibility: The Role of Companies in Supporting Democracy
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of Corporate Democratic Responsibility (CDR) and its practical application through Corporate Democratic Education (CDE), exploring how businesses can actively contribute to safeguarding the integrity and stability of democratic societies. As democracy faces increasing challenges-such as political disengagement, disinformation, populism, and the erosion of democratic norms-companies are expected not only to avoid undermining democracy but also to contribute proactively to its preservation. Building on Böckenförde's reflections on the preconditions of democracy and Popper's defense of the open society, CDR extends the traditional scope of Corporate Social Responsibility and Political Corporate Social Responsibility, urging companies to take purposeful roles in strengthening democratic institutions. CDE operationalizes this by promoting political literacy and fostering civic engagement among both internal and external stakeholders, ensuring that businesses play a pivotal role in cultivating a more informed and resilient citizenry. The paper concludes with a call for future research on the implications of CDR and CDE for CSR and the evolving role of businesses in shaping public discourse in democracies. Given the increasing threats to democratic systems, deepening our understanding of these concepts is crucial for both academic inquiry and guiding business practices, helping organizations contribute to democracy's resilience.

title: Has the Arday Affair Damaged British Trust in Universities?

detail.title: Has the Arday Affair Damaged British Trust in Universities?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest

detail.abstract:
This report produces new survey evidence on trust in UK higher education. Specifically, it asks whether the case of Jason Arday - a Cambridge professor in the Sociology of Education who was exposed as a plagiarist in late July 2026, resigned from Cambridge amid a press furore on August 5, and is believed to have committed suicide on August 14 - affected British trust in higher education.

The report finds that Britons who support Reform or the Conservatives, and who are very aware of the Arday scandal, are significantly less trusting of social science and humanities (SSH) professors than Reform and Tory voters who are not aware of the story. Right voters who are aware of the Arday story are also less trusting of universities. Left voter trust in universities or SSH professors appears to be unaffected by exposure to the story. Voters in general also remain as trusting of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) professors, with right voter awareness of the scandal not associated with lower trust in STEM professors.

title: The Paradox of Similar Reviews: How Do More Certain Review Writers Make Review Readers Less Certain?
affiliations: Manning School of Business, University of Massachusetts, Lowell and

detail.title: The Paradox of Similar Reviews: How Do More Certain Review Writers Make Review Readers Less Certain?
detail.abstract: Recognizing the role of attitude certainty in enhancing customer experience, firms often invite more certain customers to leave product reviews, assuming that writer certainty will increase readers’ certainty. By examining review platforms from both the reader and the writer perspectives, and treating sets of reviews as the unit of analysis rather than a single review, the current research challenges this notion and reveals a paradoxical reversal: we find that product review writers who are certain in their product attitudes tend to write reviews that are less similar in their language to other reviews. However, those same product reviews are likely to make readers less certain about the product because lower repetition elicits lower sense of validity. A multi-method approach involving textual analysis of a large dataset, a field study and controlled experiments demonstrate this reversal of the link between attitude certainty and repetition. Further, by uncovering how the link between language repetition and attitude certainty for writers and readers of product reviews leads to unintended influence of similar reviews, our work challenges a common misconception and highlights managerial implications to improve customer experience.

title: Performance of Monte Carlo and Collapsed Cone Algorithms for Dose Calculation in Lung Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy: Accuracy in Small Photon Fields
affiliations: Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Northwestern University - Northwestern Memorial Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Hamedan University of Medical Sciences, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Tehran University of Medical Sciences

detail.title: Performance of Monte Carlo and Collapsed Cone Algorithms for Dose Calculation in Lung Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy: Accuracy in Small Photon Fields
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Effective radiation therapy hinges on accurate dosimetry, especially in stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT). Treatment planning system (TPS) must accurately calculate doses, but uncertainties arise with lung inhomogeneity. Accuracy of Monte Carlo (MC) and Collapsed Cone (CC) algorithms have been less studied for small photon fields.Methods: This study compared MC and CC point doses with EBT3 film measurements in homogeneous and inhomogeneous phantoms across field sizes (0.5×0.5 cm² to 10×10 cm²) and photon energies (6, 10, and 18 MV). Inhomogeneity correction factors were compared between the algorithms and measurements at depths of dmax, 5, 10, 15, and 20 cm for all energies and field sizes.Results: Both MC and CC algorithms are expected to achieve above 95% accuracy in the water. However, for a very small field of 0.5×0.5 cm², the MC algorithm may be associated with on average 4.7%, 9.5%, and 10.7% dose underestimation for 6, 10, and 18 MV photons, respectively. If the CC algorithm was used in this case, it represented 13.4%, 12.0%, and 23.1%, respectively. In the inhomogeneous phantom, for field sizes ≥ 5×5 cm², the dose calculation uncertainty with the MC calculation was within 5%. As the field size decreases and the depth within the inhomogeneity increases, the value rises dramatically to ~15% and ~30% for MC and CC algorithms, respectively.Conclusions: CC algorithm should be avoided for small lesions, even outside the lung. MC algorithm is recommended for dose calculations in lung SBRT with caution, increasing the minimum IMRT/VMAT segment width to more than 0.5 cm.

title: Physician Scheduling in a Two-Tier Healthcare System with Carry-Over Mechanism
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Physician Scheduling in a Two-Tier Healthcare System with Carry-Over Mechanism
detail.abstract: This paper addresses a real-world physician scheduling problem arising from acity healthcare system comprising a Designated Central Hub and multiple Satellite Centers. We propose an optimization framework that integrates three novelfeatures: (i) a two-tier scheduling structure capturing the asymmetry between facilities that operate only during day shifts and a hub providing 24/7 coverage, (ii)a carry-over fairness mechanism that compensates physicians for surplus or deficithours from previous months, and (iii) heterogeneous holiday weighting that differentiates culturally significant occasions from ordinary holidays. The problem isformulated as a mixed-integer program with a minimax objective balancing overallworkload equity and holiday-specific equity. We present a scalable genetic algorithm with local search for solving the problem. Through a real-world case study ofa 32-physician system and extensive computational experiments, we demonstratea 48% reduction in maximum workload deviation and a 44% reduction in standard deviation compared to manual scheduling practices currently employed bythe healthcare system. Our framework provides healthcare administrators with aflexible, implementable tool for equitable physician rostering.

title: Compulsory Schooling Mitigates Health Inequality: Anthropometric Evidence from Two Centuries of Height Data
affiliations: , University of Regensburg - Department of Economics and Econometrics, Sapienza University of Rome and London School of Economics

detail.title: Compulsory Schooling Mitigates Health Inequality: Anthropometric Evidence from Two Centuries of Height Data
detail.abstract: Although compulsory education (CE) laws have widened access to schooling and shaped economic, social, and health outcomes, it remains unclear whether they reduce long-run health inequalities. We study the effect of CE policies on health inequality using height Gini indices for 66 countries between 1810 and 2000, estimating intent-to-treat effects through a staggered difference-in-differences design. Our results indicate that CE exposure reduces the height Gini. The inequality-reducing effect appears to operate mainly through increased years of schooling and reduced fertility. The effect is not uniform across regions, being largest in Europe, and it is driven largely by later extensions of CE duration rather than initial adoption alone. Overall, the findings indicate that education policy can meaningfully narrow health disparities over time, but its effectiveness depends on the scale of the mandate and the timing of adoption.

title: Long-Run Inflation and Financial Panics
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: Long-Run Inflation and Financial Panics
detail.abstract: We study how long-run inflation affects systemic bank-run risk in a medium-scale New Keynesian model with banks and endogenous financial panics. In the benchmark calibration, the bank-run probability more than doubles when annual trend inflation increases from zero to six percent. Higher trend inflation makes price-setting firms more forward-looking, thereby muting expected real-rate declines and amplifying the fall in asset prices during crises. The zero lower bound raises run risk only at low long-run inflation rates. Disinflationary transitions can sharply increase short-run risk, especially if a "cold turkey" disinflation is pursued. Finally, we discuss implications for monetary and macroprudential policy trade-offs.

title: Cultural Evolution
affiliations: Brown University - Department of Economics, University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics and University of Oxford

detail.title: Cultural Evolution
detail.abstract: What gave rise to the mosaic of cultural expressions across the globe? Why are some societies more culturally diverse than others? This study develops a unified theory of cultural evolution, characterizing the forces that have governed this process over the course of human existence. The research advances the hypothesis that population movements and socioeconomic transformations generated a mismatch between inherited cultural traits and prevailing ecological and societal conditions, setting in motion an evolutionary process governed by adaptation-based vertical transmission, horizontal diffusion, and fitness-based evolutionary selection. The theory generates novel testable predictions concerning the origins of the global cultural mosaic and the cross-societal variation in cultural diversity. First, greater ecological distance between ancestral environments generated greater cultural distance across societies. Second, prehistoric differences in ancestral diversity contributed to divergent adaptive capacity and greater cultural distance. Third, societies descended from more diverse prehistoric populations exhibit greater cultural diversity despite convergence induced by adaptation to a common environment and societal norms. Drawing on measures of cultural distance and diversity derived from folkloric and musical traditions among ethnic groups, visual representations of common concepts, and the dispersion of norms, values, and attitudes, the empirical analysis lends credence to the predictions of the theory.

title: Strategic Asset Importance and the Adoption of Data-Driven Management Practices
affiliations: , University of Nottingham and World Bank

detail.title: Strategic Asset Importance and the Adoption of Data-Driven Management Practices
detail.abstract: Quantitative measures of management quality point to wide variation in how practices are allocated within firms. We address this question by examining whether a rise in one asset’s strategic importance triggers adoption of management practices that optimize that asset. Our analysis focuses on business websites and the adoption of A/B testing, a data-driven management practice that enables firms to systematically experiment with and improve their websites. We exploit an abrupt, externally driven surge in online consumer activity as a natural experiment to identify the causal effect of a sudden rise in a digital asset’s strategic importance on adoption of this practice. Using novel monthly data on A/B testing adoption for 654,915 firms across 16 countries, we show that this sudden increase in asset importance led to a substantial rise in adoption. Adoption responses are concentrated among firms with stronger pre-existing management, data and analytics capabilities, rather than among larger or more productive firms. This is consistent with complementarities between advanced management practices and existing organizational capabilities. Finally, we find evidence that A/B testing adoption is associated with increases in revenue and labor productivity.
